topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Positional Language
topic.description: Describe the position of objects using terms such as above, below, beside, in front of, behind, next to
evidence: Describe a toy as being 'on top of' the table
Follow instructions like 'put the cube behind the box'
Use 'left' and 'right' in simple contexts
topic.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} give directions to find something around the house using words like "above," "below," "beside," "in front of," or "behind"?

pedagogy.summary: Positional language names WHERE things are relative to a landmark — on, under, behind, in front of, next to, above, below — plus the frame-dependent left and right. Children perceive these relations early and describe them with vague words ('over there', with a point); the teaching job is to attach precise words to the concepts and to model them in everyday talk. Positions are relative and abstract (whether something is 'behind' depends on the landmark and the viewer's side), so the deepest difficulties are holding two relations at once (dual relations) and left/right, which depend on the direction the child faces and are not mastered until early elementary school.
bestPractices: Model correct language in reply to vague answers: when a child says 'over there' and points, recast it — 'yes, on the shelf next to the coat closet'.
Name the landmark explicitly as object + landmark + relation ('the ball is behind the sofa') so position is heard as a relation, not a property of the object.
Embed the words in daily routines and directional games — table-setting ('cups next to the plates, juice in the middle'), hopscotch, board games with forward/back.
Build left and right on the body first (a sticker on the right hand, shaking hands) before applying them to objects; be patient and don't treat early errors as failure.
Have the child both FOLLOW and GIVE instructions ('put the cube behind the box') so the vocabulary becomes a productive tool, not just receptive.
keyRepresentations: Object–landmark–relation triples acted out with real toys and objects
The child's own body, with a right-hand sticker, for left and right
Everyday scenes — a set table, a shelf, a bedroom — and simple picture scenes to describe
Barrier games: the child describes a hidden layout precisely enough for a partner to reproduce it
commonMisconceptions: Uses vague deictic language ('over there', 'this one') with a gesture instead of a positional word
Judges left/right from the child's own current facing and cannot adjust it for an object or person facing the other way
Cannot hold two relations at once — a thing that is above one object and below another is described with only one relation (egocentrism / dual relations)
Treats a position as belonging to the object ('the front') rather than as a relation to a named landmark and a viewpoint

learn.summary: Positional language names WHERE things are relative to a landmark (on, under, behind, in front of, next to, above, below, left, right). Left/right, and behind/in front of when the landmark has no front of its own (e.g. a plain box), depend on viewpoint. Young children (4-6) perceive these relations early but describe them vaguely ('over there', with a point); the teaching job is to attach precise words to the concepts and model them in everyday talk as object + landmark + relation ('the ball is behind the sofa'). The deepest difficulties are holding two relations at once (dual relations) and left/right. Left/right for objects and for people facing you depends on viewpoint and is typically not mastered until early elementary school. Because this is a language-in-context topic, the core goal is productive AND receptive use: the child should both FOLLOW and GIVE positional instructions, not merely recognise words.

activities.title: Place the object: follow spoken positional instructions
feedback: When the relation is correct, confirm concretely: 'yes — the teddy is behind the box.'

When the object is placed in the wrong relation (e.g. beside instead of behind), show where the correct relation is from the child's own viewpoint (for a plain box, 'behind' is the side away from the child) — for example gently outline or point to the 'behind' location, then let the child try again.
Optional interactive version: a correct drop settles with a happy chime; a wrong drop highlights/outlines the target relation so 'behind' is shown, not just told.
activities.rationale: Children locate things early but must learn both the positional words and the concepts they refer to; pairing each word with a named landmark (object–landmark–relation) and acting it out is intended to make position heard as a relation rather than a property of the object.

Left and right are notoriously difficult and frame-dependent (relative to the direction the child faces), typically not mastered until early elementary school, so early failure should not be over-corrected. Holding dual relations at once (a thing above one object and below another) is hard because young children are egocentric. Everyday routines and directional games (table-setting, hopscotch, board games) build the vocabulary.
learnerActions: Listen to a spoken instruction naming an object, a landmark, and a relation, e.g. 'put the teddy behind the box'.
Move the named object into the correct relation to the landmark (for example drag it in a bedroom scene, or place a real toy with a real box and cup).
Try a short series that varies the relation: 'put the cup next to the teddy', 'put the pencil under the book'.
activities.intendedInsight: A positional word is an instruction that tells you exactly where to put something relative to a named landmark.

activities.title: Your turn to tell me: give the instruction (barrier / role-flip)
feedback: When the child names a relation and landmark the partner can act on, celebrate that the word worked: 'you said behind the box, so I put it right there.'
If the child falls back on 'there' with a gesture, recast into a usable instruction ('do you mean next to the cup?') and invite them to try the word themselves.

Optional interactive version: the child taps a relation word ('behind' / 'in front of' / 'next to'), a cartoon friend places its object to match, and the two scenes snap together when the word was right.
activities.rationale: Because the objective is both words and concepts, asking the child to produce (not just recognise) an instruction is intended to turn the vocabulary into a usable tool and to show whether the child has both the words and the concepts: a precise relation plus landmark is hard to produce by chance, so giving instructions is proposed as a way to distinguish genuine use from receptive familiarity. This production-discrimination logic is an unvalidated design proposal, not a source-established finding.

Have the partner act only on what the child says, so the child sees whether the word carried the meaning.
Play a barrier game: the child describes a hidden layout precisely enough for the partner to reproduce it without seeing it.
activities.intendedInsight: A position word is a tool that carries meaning to someone else — when I say the right relation and landmark, my partner can act correctly without seeing or pointing.

activities.title: In-role conversation: answering 'where is it?'
feedback: Recast vague deictic answers into the precise form instead of marking them wrong: 'yes — next to the cup.'
Affirm when the child supplies a relation and landmark unprompted.
activities.rationale: As a language-use topic, an in-role dialogue is intended to elicit productive spoken use and to model precise words in context (the source supports adults modelling correct language); its narrow observable limit is that it does not provide the concrete manipulate-and-see feedback of a placing game, so it complements rather than replaces that activity. Its comparative efficacy is untested.

Let the character act on the answer so the child hears whether it was clear.
Have the character gently model precise words by recasting vague answers ('over there' → 'yes, on the shelf next to the coat closet').
activities.intendedInsight: Everyday talk is where positional words become natural: naming the relation and landmark lets someone find or place a thing without seeing where you point.

activities.title: Build left and right on the body first
feedback: Reinforce correct own-body left/right with the sticker anchor.
When the child reverses left/right for a facing partner or a turned object, do not drill it as failure — acknowledge it is tricky, keep exposure, and expect later maturation.
activities.rationale: Left and right are frame-dependent and notoriously difficult, typically not mastered until early elementary school, so early errors should not be over-corrected (as the source notes). Building them on the body first with a right-hand sticker is a recommended scaffold for anchoring the terms before applying them to objects; this specific method comes from the row's best-practice synthesis rather than being prescribed by the source.

learnerActions: Put a sticker on the right hand and use it as an anchor for 'left' and 'right'.
Play own-body directional games — shaking hands with the right hand, raising the left foot.
Later, try applying left/right to objects, with the adult expecting errors and not over-correcting.
activities.intendedInsight: Left and right start from my own body; applying them to objects and to people facing me is harder and comes later.

activities.title: Embed positional words in daily routines and games
feedback: Keep supplying positional language in routines and recast vague answers; expect precise words to firm up gradually rather than immediately.
Notice and name when the child uses a relation + landmark during a real routine.

When a target sits between two landmarks, accept the one relation the child gives and add the second in a recast ('yes, on top of the red block — and it's also under the shelf') rather than forcing both at once.
activities.rationale: Everyday routines and directional games build the vocabulary in meaningful context and give repeated authentic practice across varied scenes, as the source notes.

constraints: The core objective is productive AND receptive USE: the child must both follow and give instructions. Recognition-only tasks (matching or categorising position words to pictures) can check recognition but do not by themselves elicit independent production, so they cannot alone demonstrate mastery of this language-in-context topic — use them, if at all, only as a recognition check.

Tapping a static picture scene to reveal position words is useful for exposure, but on its own it does not let the child produce instructions or receive manipulate-and-see feedback; treat it as a scaffold, not the full objective. This is a scope limit, not a claim that static images cannot teach.

Do not mark vague deictic language ('over there', 'this one' with a point) as an error for 4-6 year olds: informal language normally precedes precise words. Recast and keep supplying positional language, expecting it to firm up over time.

Do not drill left/right for facing partners/turned objects as failure, and do not force two relations (above AND below) at once: both are developmentally hard and typically not mastered until early elementary school. Accept one relation and add the second in a recast.

A rotatable 3D scene could make frame-dependence (how behind/in front and left/right flip as you move around) felt, but that perspective-taking is the hard part not expected at 4-6 and exceeds the core naming goal; it is an optional enrichment, not required.

Always pair a position word with a named landmark. Move the object to new places to show that position is a relation to the landmark, not a fixed feature of the object. As light, optional enrichment, moving the viewer around a landmark with no front of its own (e.g. a plain box) can show that 'behind' depends on where you stand. For landmarks with their own front (a sofa, a person), 'behind' usually means the landmark's own back.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of a saved teaching-research row without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The single cited source (DREME Network / Stanford) supports the general principles (model language, use object–landmark–relation, left/right and dual relations are developmentally late, use routines/games). It does not establish the comparative efficacy of any specific activity format (placing game vs. dialogue vs. 3D scene); legacy catalog claims such as 'a static image cannot teach' or '3D exceeds the goal' have been softened to scoped affordance/limit statements.

The production-discriminates-mastery logic (activity 2) and the efficacy of the dialogue format (activity 3) come from the original row's own assessment analysis and remain untested proposals; efficacy wording has been qualified accordingly.
The body-first-with-sticker scaffold for left/right (activity 4) is from the row's best-practice synthesis; the source supports only the late-mastery and patience principle, not this specific method.
Receptive-only formats are limited only in the narrow, observable sense that recognition does not itself elicit production — this is not a claim about which medium is superior.

probeDeeper: You told me the teddy is 'there' — if I close my eyes, can you tell me a word so I know exactly where it is without pointing?
You said it's on your left. If I come and sit on the other side of the table, is it still on my left?
The pencil is on top of the book. Is anything above the pencil too?
Put the cube 'behind' the box — now if you turn the box around, is the cube still behind it?
assess.correctAnswer: Follows each positional instruction by placing the object in the correct relation, and, when giving the instruction, uses a precise positional word (behind / next to / on top of / under) together with a named landmark, so the teacher can act on it unambiguously — not a vague 'there' with a point.

errorPatterns.pattern: Says 'over there' or 'this one' with a point instead of a position word ('put it... there!')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do NOT mark this as an error — vague informal language normally precedes precise words; recast it ('yes, next to the cup') and keep supplying positional language in routines, expecting it to firm up over time.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: When GIVING an instruction, gestures or says 'there' rather than naming a relation

errorPatterns.pattern: Uses left/right fixed to their own body, so it is wrong for an object or a person facing the other way ('it's on the left' — but only from where I'm sitting)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do NOT drill this as a failure — left/right is frame-dependent and typically not mastered until early elementary school; reinforce own-body left/right (sticker) and keep exposure, expecting later maturation.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Gives or follows left/right correctly for self but reverses it for a facing partner or a turned object

errorPatterns.pattern: Cannot say a thing is above one object and below another at the same time ('it's on top' — ignoring what is above it)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do NOT push both relations at once — accept the one they give and add the second in your recast ('yes, on top of the red block — and it's also under the shelf'), letting the coordination develop.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: When a target sits between two landmarks, describes only one relation

errorPatterns.pattern: Treats a position word as a fixed feature of the object rather than a relation to a landmark ('the front', with no reference to what it is in front of)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Always pair the word with a named landmark and physically move the viewer or the object to show that 'behind' changes with viewpoint.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Names a position with no landmark, or insists 'behind' is a fixed side of the object regardless of the viewer

responseLevels.gap: Relies on gesture and 'there / this one'; follows only the most familiar single instruction; cannot produce a usable positional instruction.
responseLevels.full: Uses precise positional words productively and receptively across new scenes, names the landmark, and begins to coordinate two relations and adjust for viewpoint (relational) — with a full grasp of left/right for others expected only later.
responseLevels.partial: Follows and produces common single relations (on / under / behind / next to) with a named landmark in simple familiar setups, but breaks down on left/right for a facing partner, on dual relations, or in an unfamiliar scene — handling one relation at a time without coordinating them (multistructural).

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Set up a real or pictured scene with a box, a toy and a cup. Give a short series of doing-instructions and one telling task, and watch/listen for USE: 'Put the teddy behind the box. ... Now put the cup next to the teddy. ... Now YOU tell me where to put the pencil, so I can do exactly what you say.'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who has both the words and the concepts follows correctly AND produces a usable instruction that names a relation and a landmark. A child with only receptive familiarity may follow simple cases but, when asked to give an instruction, falls back on 'there' with a gesture or names the object with no relation — revealing the word is not yet a tool. Requiring production is the discriminator: a precise relation cannot be produced by luck.

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Position, direction, and movement
topic.description: Use mathematical vocabulary to describe position, direction, and movement, including straight lines and distinguishing rotation as a turn in terms of right angles (quarter, half, three-quarter turns, clockwise and anti-clockwise)
evidence: Use terms such as clockwise, anti-clockwise, quarter turn, half turn, three-quarter turn
Describe a right angle as a quarter turn
Give and follow directions involving straight-line movement and turns
topic.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} follow directions like "turn clockwise a quarter turn" or "move three squares to the right" on a grid or in a simple navigation game?

pedagogy.summary: Year 2 sharpens the movement vocabulary: children add clockwise and anti-clockwise to whole, half, quarter and three-quarter turns, link a quarter turn to a right angle, and give and follow multi-step directions combining straight-line moves with turns. The words are to be used, not defined — the aim is fluent, correct use in routes and turn descriptions. Clockwise/anti-clockwise is a new convention layered onto the still-developing left/right, and the quarter-turn = right-angle link is the crucial bridge to the formal angle work that follows.
bestPractices: Introduce clockwise from a real clock's hands, then transfer it to the body and to turning objects, contrasting it explicitly with anti-clockwise each time.
Make the quarter-turn = right-angle link concrete: turn a quarter and mark the right angle between the start and finish arms (an angle is an amount of turn shown by two adjoining lines).
Combine moves and turns into routes to give and follow (barrier games, floor robots) so the vocabulary is productive.
Keep turns embodied and referenced to target facings before moving to described or drawn routes.
Continue supporting left/right on the body and expect residual errors as frame-dependence is still developing.
keyRepresentations: A clock face for clockwise and anti-clockwise
Body or floor-robot turns with start/finish facings, and the right-angle mark left by a quarter turn
Route maps and grids to describe and to follow with combined moves and turns
Two adjoining arms (the start and finish of a turn) showing the angle turned through
commonMisconceptions: Clockwise and anti-clockwise confused with each other or with left/right — a new convention on top of frame-dependent left/right
A quarter turn not connected to a right angle — the two treated as separate, unrelated facts
Turn amounts miscounted — a half or a quarter turn produced when a three-quarter turn is asked for
Egocentric direction-giving: routes given from the child's own viewpoint without accounting for the follower's facing

learn.summary: Year 2 children use (not merely define) movement vocabulary: clockwise and anti-clockwise added to whole, half, quarter and three-quarter turns; a quarter turn linked to a right angle; and multi-step directions combining straight-line moves with turns that another person can actually follow. Clockwise/anti-clockwise is a new convention layered on still-developing left/right, and the quarter-turn = right-angle link bridges to later formal angle work. Guidance keeps turns embodied and routes followable, with feedback on wrong direction or amount.

activities.title: Clockwise, anti-clockwise and the right angle a quarter turn leaves
feedback: If a child turns the wrong way on a clockwise/anti-clockwise instruction, return to a real clock's hand direction as the anchor and label both ways explicitly each time.
If a child makes the quarter turn but cannot name or denies the right angle, mark the right angle between the start and finish arms every single time until the link becomes automatic.
When a child miscounts the turn amount (e.g. a half or quarter turn when a three-quarter turn was asked), count the quarter turns aloud — one, two, three — marking each right angle as it is passed.
Confirm when two clockwise quarter turns are recognised as a half turn, reinforcing that quarters accumulate.
activities.rationale: The curriculum expects pupils to distinguish rotation as a turn and in terms of right angles for quarter, half and three-quarter turns, clockwise and anti-clockwise. An angle is an amount of turn shown by two adjoining lines, and the dynamic (turn) and static (corner) conceptions of a right angle must be brought together, which marking the arms of a quarter turn supports. A manipulable clock/dial with a stamped right angle makes the mechanism concrete; a fixed diagram can still illustrate the link but cannot be turned by the child.
sourceClaims: Year 2 pupils should use mathematical vocabulary to describe position, direction and movement, including movement in a straight line and distinguishing between rotation as a turn and in terms of right angles for quarter, half and three-quarter turns (clockwise and anti-clockwise).

An angle is an amount of turn represented by two adjoining lines (start and finish positions); children develop right angles as quarter turns by turning with one arm fixed while the other moves, linking turn to the right angle formed — the static (corner) and dynamic (turn) conceptions must come together.
learnerActions: Watch a real clock's hands and name the direction they travel as 'clockwise'; then turn your own body a quarter turn clockwise (towards your right, the way the hands would go on a clock lying face-up on the floor and seen from above) and say where you now face.
Make a quarter turn clockwise and mark or point out the corner (angle) between where you started facing and where you finish facing; name it as a right angle.
Make the same quarter turn anti-clockwise and describe how the finishing facing differs.

On a clock face or turn dial, spin an arrow with a 'clockwise, quarter turn' control so it moves 90° and leaves a right-angle mark between start and finish; use 'anti-clockwise' to send it back the other way.
Make two quarter turns clockwise in a row and decide whether that equals one half turn, counting each quarter aloud.
Make a three-quarter turn clockwise, counting the quarters, and point out that three right angles have been passed.
activities.intendedInsight: A quarter turn always leaves a right angle between the start and finish arms, and clockwise versus anti-clockwise decides which way you turn — turning fuzzy words into exact instructions.

activities.title: Give and follow a multi-step route that someone else can act on
feedback: If a child gives directions from their own viewpoint so 'turn left' is wrong for the follower, do NOT treat it as a failure: walk the route exactly as they said so they SEE the mismatch, then model taking the follower's view. De-centring matures with age.
When a robot hits a wall, name whether the direction or the amount of turn was wrong and let the child re-string the instruction.
Probe with 'turn that quarter anti-clockwise this time — where do you face now?' to check the direction convention under a new turn.
Ask 'when you say turn left, is that your left or mine?' to surface the follower's frame of reference.
activities.rationale: Giving and following directions that combine straight-line movement and turns makes the vocabulary productive rather than merely recognised. Left/right and route-taking are frame-dependent and late-developing; young children are egocentric and find it hard to imagine a route from another's viewpoint, so making the follower act it out literally is a developmental support, not a test to pass. Immediate feedback on wrong direction or amount (a wall, a mismatch walked out) ties the words to consequences.
sourceClaims: Year 2 pupils should use mathematical vocabulary to describe position, direction and movement, including movement in a straight line and distinguishing between rotation as a turn and in terms of right angles for quarter, half and three-quarter turns (clockwise and anti-clockwise).

Left and right are frame-dependent (relative to the direction the child faces) and late-developing; young children are egocentric and find it hard to de-center and imagine how a space or route looks from another point of view, which they master only as they get older.
learnerActions: Guide a partner (or a floor robot) from one point to another using a sequence such as 'forward 2, turn clockwise quarter, forward 3', combining straight-line moves with named turns.
Have the follower act out the route exactly as given, from the follower's own facing, and watch what happens.
On a grid, drive a programmable robot through a maze by stringing moves and turns; a wrong turn direction or wrong amount sends it into a wall, prompting a correction.
Play a barrier game: describe a route to someone who cannot see your map, using direction and turn words precisely enough for them to reproduce it.
When a route 'goes wrong', revise the instructions so the follower, not just you, can reach the target.
activities.intendedInsight: Direction and turn words are most useful when they form a sequence another person can follow from their own viewpoint — producing a followable route is the real goal.

activities.title: Check and sort turn and route language
feedback: If a selection is wrong, re-make the turn physically and compare the finishing facing.
For a mismatched quarter-turn/right-angle pairing, mark the angle between start and finish arms and compare.
Treat recognition choices as a check only; always follow with giving or following a live route so the child constructs instructions, not just identifies them.
activities.rationale: Selecting a facing, matching a quarter turn to a right angle, and sequencing a route give a reliable, quick check of the vocabulary. Such recognition tasks confirm what a child can identify but do not by themselves elicit the child's own construction of turns and routes, so they supplement rather than replace the embodied and productive activities above.
learnerActions: After a stated clockwise or anti-clockwise quarter turn, pick which direction you now face from given options.
Match a quarter turn to one right angle, a half turn to two right angles, and a three-quarter turn to three right angles.
Put a jumbled set of move-and-turn instructions into the order that reaches a target, then test the order by walking or driving it.
activities.intendedInsight: You can recognise correct turn facings and the quarter-turn/right-angle link quickly, then confirm sequences by acting them out.

constraints: The goal is fluent, correct USE of the words in routes and turn descriptions, not reciting definitions.
Keep turns embodied and referenced to target facings before moving to described or drawn routes.
Introduce clockwise from a real clock's hands, then transfer to the body and to turning objects, contrasting it explicitly with anti-clockwise each time.
Continue supporting left/right on the body and expect residual errors: frame-dependence is still developing at this age.
Egocentric direction-giving is developmentally expected, not a failure; surface it by having the follower act the route out literally rather than correcting abstractly.

Recognition/selection and matching tasks can check the vocabulary but do not by themselves elicit the child producing turns and followable routes, so the child must still construct turns and routes themselves.

A fixed picture or diagram can illustrate the quarter-turn/right-angle link but cannot be turned by the child; a manipulable dial or embodied turn supplies the dynamic experience. Neither claim is that a static image 'cannot teach' the idea.

Interactive controls (clockwise/anti-clockwise and quarter/half buttons, a stamped right-angle mark, a robot that hits a wall on a wrong move) are optional ways to make feedback concrete, not required mechanisms.
Rendering turns and routes in 3D is optional; the ideas are planar and do not require it.

Self-audit of arithmetic: a quarter turn = one right angle (90°); two quarter turns = one half turn (180°) = two right angles; a three-quarter turn = three right angles. These were checked and are correct. The three-quarter-turn mis-count example (producing a half or quarter instead) is retained as an error pattern, not taught as correct.

The original source row rated open conversation as a 'poor' fit and framed a recognition/selection artefact as assessing 'without building the doing'; these are framed here as scope limits (recognition does not by itself elicit construction) rather than universal claims that dialogue or static media cannot teach.

Legacy comparative framing ('a static picture cannot deliver', '3D adds little') has been softened to stated affordances/limits without asserting new efficacy comparisons, since the exact sources do not establish necessity or comparative effectiveness.

errorPatterns.nextMove: Return to a real clock's hand direction as the anchor and label both ways explicitly each time.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Turns the wrong direction on a clockwise or anti-clockwise instruction

errorPatterns.pattern: Does not link a quarter turn to a right angle — treats 'quarter turn' and 'right angle' as unrelated
errorPatterns.nextMove: Mark the right angle between the start and finish arms of the quarter turn every single time until the link is automatic.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Makes a quarter turn but cannot name the angle turned through, or denies that it is a right angle

errorPatterns.pattern: Miscounts the turn amount — produces a half or a quarter turn when a three-quarter turn is asked for
errorPatterns.nextMove: Count the quarter turns aloud (one, two, three), marking each right angle as it is passed.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The finish facing after the requested turn is wrong

errorPatterns.pattern: Gives directions from own viewpoint without adjusting for the follower's facing, so 'turn left' is wrong for the person following
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do NOT treat as a failure — walk it exactly as they said so they SEE the mismatch, and model taking the follower's view; de-centring matures with age.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: When you follow their route exactly from your own facing, the turns come out wrong

responseLevels.gap: Confuses clockwise and anti-clockwise, does not link a quarter turn to a right angle, and gives unfollowable or purely egocentric routes.
responseLevels.full: Uses clockwise / anti-clockwise and quarter / half / three-quarter turns correctly, names a quarter turn as a right angle, and gives and follows multi-step routes combining moves and turns that another person can act on, transferring to new routes (relational) — beginning to adjust for the follower's viewpoint.
responseLevels.partial: Uses quarter and half turns and follows single instructions, and can echo clockwise and right-angle language, but turns the wrong way on clockwise/anti-clockwise, does not spontaneously name the quarter turn as a right angle, or gives routes only from their own viewpoint (multistructural).

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give a context and listen for USE: 'Face the window. Make a quarter turn clockwise — which way did you go, and what is the angle you turned through? ... Now guide me from the door to your chair, telling me every move and every turn.' Listen for correct use of clockwise / anti-clockwise, quarter / half / three-quarter, right angle, and a route someone could actually follow.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Combining clockwise with a turn amount, then requiring the right-angle naming and a followable route, separates a child who uses the vocabulary as precise instructions from one who parrots the words but turns the wrong way, omits the right-angle link, or gives an egocentric route. Producing a route the teacher can actually follow is the discriminator.

sources.claim: Year 2 pupils should use mathematical vocabulary to describe position, direction and movement, including movement in a straight line and distinguishing between rotation as a turn and in terms of right angles for quarter, half and three-quarter turns (clockwise and anti-clockwise).

sources.claim: An angle is an amount of turn represented by two adjoining lines (start and finish positions); children develop right angles as quarter turns by turning with one arm fixed while the other moves, linking turn to the right angle formed — the static (corner) and dynamic (turn) conceptions must come together.

sources.claim: Left and right are frame-dependent (relative to the direction the child faces) and late-developing; young children are egocentric and find it hard to de-center and imagine how a space or route looks from another point of view, which they master only as they get older.

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Coordinates (age 8+)
topic.description: Plot specified points on a coordinate grid and draw sides to complete a given polygon
evidence: Plot points (1,1), (1,4), (5,4), (5,1) and join to make a rectangle
Given three vertices of a square, plot the fourth vertex
Complete a triangle by plotting the third vertex at given coordinates and drawing sides
topic.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is given three coordinate pairs on a grid, can they plot each point and then connect the dots to draw the correct triangle or rectangle?

pedagogy.summary: This topic turns coordinate reading into PRODUCING: given coordinates, plot the point on the grid; and given a shape's structure, work out and plot a missing vertex, then draw the sides. It is a two-way translation between the symbolic pair (x, y) and the spatial mark on the grid — reading a pair to place a point, and reading a placed configuration to generate a new coordinate. Completing a polygon (find the 4th vertex of a square, the 3rd of a triangle) is where coordinates meet shape properties: the missing vertex of a rectangle/square shares one known vertex's x-value and another's y-value. The dominant error, as in reading, is reversal (plotting up-then-across); the second is completing a shape 'by eye' from appearance rather than reasoning from the coordinates.
bestPractices: Plot with the same along-then-up discipline as reading: find the x-line first, travel up to the y-line, mark the intersection — count from the origin against numbered lines.

For a missing vertex, reason from coordinates and shape properties, not appearance: the 4th vertex of a rectangle takes its x from one neighbour and its y from the other; verify sides are the right lengths.
Have children state the missing coordinate BEFORE plotting it, so the reasoning is explicit and checkable.
Draw the sides in order and check the result is the intended polygon (right angles for a rectangle, equal sides for a square), catching mis-plotted vertices.
Contrast a correctly completed square with a plausible-looking wrong one to show that 'looks right' is not the test — the coordinates are.
Use the reversal distractor deliberately: plot (5,4) and (4,5) to show they are different, reinforcing order in the act of plotting.
keyRepresentations: Numbered coordinate grid with origin, points plotted as line-intersections
Along-then-up plotting path from the origin to each point
Partly-drawn polygon with given vertices and one missing, to be completed
The missing vertex sharing one neighbour's x and another neighbour's y (rectangle/square)
Completed shape with all vertex coordinates labelled
commonMisconceptions: Reversal when plotting — going up before across, so the point lands in the mirror position (e.g. plots (5,4) at 4-across-5-up).
Completing a polygon by eye/appearance rather than reasoning from coordinates and shape properties, giving a wrong missing vertex.
Counting squares instead of numbered lines when plotting, producing off-by-one positions.
Joining vertices in the wrong order, producing a crossed or incorrect polygon even when the points are right.

learn.summary: This topic moves children from reading coordinates to PRODUCING them: given a pair (x, y), plot the point; given a partly-drawn polygon, reason out and plot a missing vertex, then draw the sides. The key reasoning is that the missing vertex of a rectangle or square whose sides run along the grid lines shares one neighbour's x-value and another neighbour's y-value, so completion is derived from coordinates and shape properties rather than guessed by eye. The two dominant errors are reversal (plotting up-then-across) and completing 'by eye' from appearance instead of reasoning from the coordinates.

activities.title: Plot-and-complete on a numbered grid
feedback: If a plotted point lands reversed, return to along-then-up plotting from the origin, tie the first number to the across axis, and plot (5,1) and (1,5) together to show they differ.
If the fourth vertex is placed by eye (near but not at the target), ask the child to say which neighbour's x and which neighbour's y it must share, then check side lengths and right angles.
If points land one line off, anchor at the origin (0,0) and count the numbered line labels aloud while placing the point, rather than counting cells crossed.

When the drawn sides form a leaning or lopsided quadrilateral, point out that the coordinates, side lengths and right angles, not the appearance, are the test — four equal sides and four right angles for a square, equal opposite sides and four right angles for a rectangle.
activities.rationale: Plotting and completing a polygon is a produce-and-check action: entering a point and drawing the sides gives spatial feedback that exposes reversal (the point visibly lands wrong) and by-eye completion (the figure fails to close into the named shape, or the side lengths are unequal). Stating the coordinate before plotting makes the reasoning explicit and checkable.
sourceClaims: Students graph points in the first quadrant to represent problems and interpret coordinate values, locating each point by an ordered pair measured from the origin along the two axes (5.G.1, 5.G.2).
Year 4 pupils should plot specified points and draw sides to complete a given polygon.

A common documented misconception is putting the y-coordinate before the x, giving an incorrectly placed point; the Year 4 objective works on a grid where the lines are numbered (reading numbered lines rather than counting squares). Sample key questions ask for the missing fourth vertex of a square given three vertices.
learnerActions: Plot a given point by finding the x-line first, travelling up to the y-line, and marking the intersection, counting from the origin against the numbered lines.
Plot (5,4) and then (4,5) and compare: show they land in different places to make the along-then-up order explicit.

Given three vertices of a genuine square, e.g. (1,1), (1,4) and (4,4) (whose fourth vertex is (4,1), a 3-by-3 square with four equal sides), STATE the fourth coordinate aloud before plotting it, then plot it and draw the sides; check all four side lengths are equal and all four corners are right angles so the figure is genuinely a square.
Check the completed figure is the intended polygon: right angles and matching opposite sides for a rectangle, right angles and four equal sides for a square.

Repeat with three vertices of a rectangle, e.g. (1,1), (1,4), (5,4) whose fourth vertex is (5,1), giving a 4-by-3 rectangle, so the shared-x / shared-y reasoning transfers and children see that unequal sides (4 and 3) make a rectangle, not a square.
activities.intendedInsight: A point's location is fixed by reading x (across) then y (up) from the origin, and the missing vertex of a rectangle or square whose sides run along the grid lines can be reasoned out because it shares one neighbour's x and another neighbour's y; 'looks right' is replaced by 'is right' when the drawn sides form the named shape, with right angles at every corner and matching side lengths — four equal sides for a square, equal opposite sides for a rectangle.

activities.title: Which coordinate completes the shape? — diagnostic choices
feedback: If the reversed pair is chosen, revisit along-then-up order and compare the swapped pair with the correct one on a grid.
If the by-eye value is chosen, ask which neighbour supplies the x and which supplies the y for the missing corner, then check the side lengths.
If points are joined in the wrong order producing a crossed figure, draw the sides in vertex order and check the shape closes correctly.
activities.rationale: Choosing the correct missing vertex is cleanly scorable and useful for diagnosis, with the reversed pair and the by-eye value as targeted distractors. On its own this recognition format does not elicit the child independently plotting and drawing to see the sides close, so pair it with a grid where the child produces and checks.
sourceClaims: A common documented misconception is putting the y-coordinate before the x, giving an incorrectly placed point; the Year 4 objective works on a grid where the lines are numbered (reading numbered lines rather than counting squares). Sample key questions ask for the missing fourth vertex of a square given three vertices.
learnerActions: Choose which coordinate completes a given genuine square, e.g. three vertices (1,1),(1,4),(4,4) whose correct fourth vertex is (4,1), from options that include the reversed pair and a plausible but wrong by-eye value.
Explain WHY the chosen coordinate is correct in terms of shared x and shared y, not appearance.
Match a set of plotted points to their coordinate labels.
Plot a given set of points to form a rectangle and join them in order.
activities.intendedInsight: Identifying the correct missing vertex, and rejecting the reversal and by-eye distractors, shows that the vertex is determined by the coordinates and shape structure, not by how the figure looks.

activities.title: Reveal how a completed shape's coordinates relate
feedback: If a prediction is wrong, show which neighbour supplies the x and which supplies the y and re-trace the plotting path.
Prompt the child to state the shared-value reasoning before revealing the answer so the pattern, not the picture, is used.
activities.rationale: A static or worked grid can display the structural relationship between vertices and let the child predict before revealing, which supports the shared-x/shared-y reasoning. It is a scaffold: a fixed figure cannot be re-plotted or tested by the child, so the producing that defines this topic still needs an interactive or paper grid where the child plots their own points and draws the sides.
sourceClaims: Year 4 pupils should plot specified points and draw sides to complete a given polygon.
learnerActions: On a completed rectangle with all vertices labelled, tap each corner to reveal how its coordinates relate to its neighbours (which x it shares, which y it shares).
Before a 'where must the fourth corner go?' answer is revealed, predict the coordinate and give a reason based on the shared values.
Trace the along-then-up path from the origin to each labelled vertex.
activities.intendedInsight: Even on a worked, labelled figure the child can see the structural pattern — each vertex shares an x with one neighbour and a y with another — which is the reasoning needed to complete a polygon.

constraints: Plot with along-then-up discipline: find the x-line, travel up to the y-line, mark the intersection; count from the origin against the numbered lines, not by counting squares.

Completion must be reasoned from coordinates and shape properties (shared x and shared y of neighbours, for shapes whose sides run along the grid lines), not from appearance; verify side lengths and right angles — four equal sides with four right angles confirm a square, equal opposite sides with four right angles a rectangle.
Have children state the missing coordinate before plotting it so the reasoning is explicit and checkable.

Recognition-only formats (choosing the missing vertex, matching labels) are good for diagnosis but do not by themselves show the child independently plotting and drawing the sides to see the figure close; pair them with a produce-and-draw task.
A worked, labelled figure is a scaffold: it shows the relationship but cannot be re-plotted or tested by the child, so include a grid (interactive or paper) where the child plots and draws.
First-quadrant plotting and completing plane polygons is a 2D task; include the zero-coordinate/axis case, e.g. compare (3,0) and (0,3) as distinct points.

When a point set is named a square, confirm it actually has four equal sides; a set like (1,1),(1,4),(5,4),(5,1) has unequal sides (4 and 3) and is a rectangle, so use it as a rectangle example and reserve 'square' for equal-sided sets such as (1,1),(1,4),(4,4),(4,1).
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Optional interaction examples retained from the source (type a coordinate to drop a point with an along-then-up trail, snap-to-numbered-lines with origin highlighted, a complete-the-polygon mode that draws the sides and names the resulting shape, (5,4) vs (4,5) order check) are illustrative of the learning mechanism and are not mandatory.

The source's '3D adds no value' and 'dialogue cannot teach plotting' claims were not propagated as universal laws; 2D plotting is the natural medium for this content, but no comparative-efficacy claim is asserted.

Corrected original error: the point set (1,1), (1,4), (5,4) with fourth vertex (5,1) forms a RECTANGLE 4 units wide and 3 units tall (sides 4 and 3), NOT a square. The derivation is sound — the fourth vertex shares x=5 with (5,4) and y=1 with (1,1) — but the original row's diagnostic prompt and correctAnswer mislabel the resulting figure a 'square' (its own evidence list correctly calls the identical set a rectangle). Guidance now treats this set as a rectangle example and supplies a genuine square example (1,1),(1,4),(4,4),(4,1), a 3-by-3 square with four equal sides.

probeDeeper: 'How did you know the fourth corner was (5,1) and not somewhere else?' — listen for 'it shares this x and that y', not 'it looked right'.
Counterexample: 'If I move this corner from (5,1) to (5,2), is it still a square? Why not?' — tests that the coordinates, not appearance, define the shape.
'Here are three corners of a rectangle instead of a square — where does the fourth go?' — checks the shared-x/shared-y reasoning transfers.
'Plot (3,0) and (0,3) — are they the same point?' — surfaces order and the zero-coordinate/axis case during producing.
assess.correctAnswer: READ: each point is located across (x) then up (y) from the origin — e.g. (5,4) is 5 across, 4 up. PRODUCE: the fourth vertex is (5,1) — it shares the x-value (5) of (5,4) and the y-value (1) of (1,1); plotted at 5-across-1-up, completing the square with vertical and horizontal sides.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reversal when plotting — plots the fourth vertex (or reads a given one) up-before-across, placing (5,1) at 1-across-5-up.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Return to along-then-up plotting from the origin, tying the first number to the x (across) axis; plot (5,1) and (1,5) together to show they differ.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The plotted point is the coordinate-swap of the correct one; the drawn figure is not a square; reading of the given vertices may also swap across and up.

errorPatterns.pattern: Completes the polygon by eye — places the fourth vertex where it 'looks right' rather than reasoning from the coordinates and the square's properties.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reason from structure: the missing vertex of a rectangle/square shares one neighbour's x and the other's y; check side lengths and right angles rather than trusting appearance.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The fourth point is near but not at (5,1); the child can't say it should share (5,4)'s x and (1,1)'s y; the drawn shape is a rough quadrilateral, not a square.

errorPatterns.pattern: Counts squares not numbered lines — plots off-by-one, or starts from 1 instead of the origin.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Anchor at the origin (0,0) and plot on the numbered lines; count line labels aloud while placing the point.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Points land one line off; the child counts cells crossed rather than reading the line labels.

responseLevels.gap: Cannot plot given points reliably or complete the polygon: points land reversed or off-by-one, no missing vertex, or a shape that isn't the target.
responseLevels.full: Reads each given vertex as (across, up), derives the missing vertex from the shared x and y of its neighbours, plots it accurately on the numbered lines, and draws sides that form the correct polygon — reading and producing coordinates fluently in both directions.
responseLevels.partial: Plots the given vertices correctly (can read the marks) but cannot PRODUCE the missing vertex by reasoning — guesses by eye, or reverses when plotting the new point — so the completed figure is not a true square; reads but does not fully translate to producing.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Show a grid with three vertices of a square marked and labelled: (1,1), (1,4) and (5,4). First (READ): 'Point to each marked vertex and tell me what its two numbers mean.' Then (PRODUCE): 'Plot the fourth vertex to complete the square, write its coordinates, and draw the sides.' Watch both the reading and the plotting.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The task requires BOTH translating a symbol to a location (reading the given vertices) and generating a new symbol from a spatial/structural constraint (the missing vertex). A child who can read but not produce plots by eye and misses (5,1); a child who reverses lands the fourth vertex at (1,5); a child reasoning correctly derives it from the shared x and y. Drawing the sides then exposes whether the figure is actually a square, catching by-appearance completion.

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Describing Movements
topic.description: Describe movements between positions as translations of a given unit to the left/right and up/down
evidence: Describe moving from (2,3) to (5,3) as 3 units to the right
Translate a shape 4 units right and 2 units up and state the new coordinates
Predict where a point will be after a given translation
topic.assessmentPrompt: If a shape is at position (2, 3) on a grid and you tell {{name}} to move it four squares right and two squares up, can they work out its new position without drawing it first?

pedagogy.summary: A translation is a slide: every point of a shape moves the same distance left/right and the same distance up/down, and nothing else changes (size, shape and orientation stay the same). This topic makes that concrete on a coordinate grid — describing the move from one position to another ('3 units right'), carrying out a two-part translation ('4 right and 2 up') and stating the new coordinates, and PREDICTING an image without plotting. The key procedural insight is that a horizontal move changes only the x-coordinate and a vertical move only the y-coordinate: right adds to x, up adds to y. Built on first-quadrant coordinates, it is the child's first taste of transformations, and its errors mirror coordinate errors — reversal (swapping the right and up amounts) and changing the wrong coordinate.
bestPractices: Separate the two components explicitly: a rightward move changes only x (add to the first number), an upward move only y (add to the second) — do the horizontal and vertical parts one at a time.
Describe moves precisely and consistently: 'units right/left and up/down', matching the along-then-up order of coordinates.
Have children PREDICT the new coordinates by adjusting x and y before plotting, then check by plotting — so the rule is used, not just the picture.
Stress translation invariance: the shape does not turn, flip, or resize — every vertex shifts by the same amounts; check two vertices moved identically.
Count moves against numbered lines from the start point, not squares, to avoid off-by-one slips.
Contrast a horizontal-only move (y unchanged) with a two-part move, so children see when a coordinate should and shouldn't change.
keyRepresentations: Coordinate grid showing a start point and its translated image with the slide arrow
Component decomposition: horizontal move (Δx) then vertical move (Δy)
Rule form: (x, y) → (x + right, y + up)
A shape and its translated copy, same size and orientation, every vertex shifted equally
Number-line counting of the move along each axis from the start position
commonMisconceptions: Reversal — swapping the right and up amounts (applying the horizontal shift to y and the vertical to x).
Changing the wrong coordinate — altering y for a move described as 'right', or changing both coordinates for a single-direction move.
Getting the direction sign wrong — moving left when 'right' is stated, or subtracting instead of adding.
Counting squares rather than numbered lines, giving an off-by-one image position.
Confusing the description of the MOVE with the destination coordinates (stating where it ends when asked how it moved, or vice versa).

learn.summary: Translation is a slide: every point of a shape moves the same amount left/right and up/down, with size, shape and orientation unchanged. On a first-quadrant coordinate grid, learners describe a move from one position to another ('3 units right'), carry out a two-part translation ('4 right and 2 up') and state new coordinates, and predict an image before plotting. The core procedural insight: a horizontal move changes only the x-coordinate (right adds to x), a vertical move only the y-coordinate (up adds to y). The main errors mirror coordinate errors — reversing the right/up amounts, changing the wrong coordinate, direction/sign slips, off-by-one line counting, and confusing the description of the move with the destination coordinates.

activities.title: Predict-then-slide on a coordinate grid
feedback: If the prediction swaps the amounts (e.g. gives (4,7) for '4 right, 2 up' from (2,3)), do the parts one at a time: right changes only the first number, up only the second — tie this back to the along-then-up order of coordinates.
If a 'right' move changed the up-number, show on the grid that a purely horizontal slide leaves the height (y) unchanged; label which number each direction affects before moving.
If the image lands one line off, recount the move as jumps from the start point: the start line is 0, and the first jump lands on the next line. Do not count the starting line as 1.
For opposite directions ('2 left, 1 down' from (5,4)), confirm left subtracts from x and down subtracts from y, landing at (3,3).
activities.rationale: Setting a move, predicting coordinates, then watching the slide turns the coordinate rule into something tested against the motion, exposing reversal and wrong-coordinate errors immediately. Live-updating coordinates, a colour-coded ('coded') grid that makes a rightward move visibly change only x, and the uniform vertex shift make the component structure (Δx separate from Δy) and translation invariance concrete. These coordinate readouts, colour-coding and the predict-then-reveal loop are optional interaction examples that make the mechanism visible, not required technology.
sourceClaims: Year 4 pupils should describe movements between positions as translations of a given unit to the left/right and up/down.
Points are located by ordered pairs from the origin along the x- and y-axes in the first quadrant, so a horizontal move changes the x-coordinate and a vertical move the y-coordinate (5.G.1, 5.G.2).

A common documented coordinate misconception is reversing x and y (putting the y-coordinate before the x), and off-by-one errors from counting squares rather than the numbered grid lines — errors that carry into describing moves as changes in coordinates.
learnerActions: Set a translation such as '4 right and 2 up' on a first-quadrant grid containing a shape.
Before anything moves, predict and state (or type) the new coordinates of one named vertex — e.g. from (2,3) you should get (6,5).
Trigger the slide and watch every vertex glide by the same 4-across, 2-up while a coordinate readout ticks from the old to the new values.
Run a horizontal-only move (e.g. '3 right') and confirm the up-number (y) stays fixed while only the across-number changes.
Check two different vertices moved by identical amounts, confirming the shape did not turn, flip or resize.
Count the move in unit jumps from the start point, without counting the starting line itself as 'one'.
activities.intendedInsight: A horizontal move changes only x and a vertical move only y; the whole shape shifts uniformly without changing size or orientation, and predicting from the (x+right, y+up) rule can be checked against the actual slide.

activities.title: Describe the move between two positions
feedback: If the move is answered with '(5,3)' instead of '3 right', ask explicitly 'how did it move?' versus 'where is it now?' and have the learner give both for the same slide.
If direction is reversed (saying 'left' for a rightward shift), compare the two numbered positions and read which way along the axis the point travelled.
activities.rationale: Requiring a worded description catches children who confuse the move with the destination, a documented pattern, and reversing the move builds the idea that translations are undoable by the opposite shift. A scorable version (multiple-choice naming the move between two points, with reversed-component and 'up' distractors) can be used during teaching or for assessment, though a selection response does not elicit independent construction of the description.
sourceClaims: Year 4 pupils should describe movements between positions as translations of a given unit to the left/right and up/down.
learnerActions: Look at two marked positions on the grid, e.g. a start at (2,3) and an image at (5,3).
State the move in words — '3 units right' — using units and direction, not the destination coordinates.
For the same slide, separately answer 'where is it now?' with the end coordinates, so the two questions are practised side by side.
Describe the reverse move that returns the image to the start (e.g. (5,3) back to (2,3) is '3 units left'), surfacing reversibility.
activities.intendedInsight: Describing a move ('how did it move?' — units and direction) is a different answer from naming the destination ('where is it now?' — coordinates); learners must hold both apart.

activities.title: Tap-to-reveal before-and-after picture (scaffold)
feedback: Point out that only the across-number changed for a horizontal slide, and that both corners moved by the same amount.
Prompt the learner to say the move in words before lifting the flap, then compare.
activities.rationale: A fixed picture can present and label a completed slide, but it cannot let the learner set, carry out or predict a move, so the procedure is not exercised — use it as an introduction or revision aid, not the main practice.
learnerActions: Study a fixed picture showing a shape in its start position and its translated image with a slide arrow.
Tap the start and the image to reveal how the x- and y-coordinates changed between them.
Use a 'where does it land after 3 right?' flap to check a predicted position against the revealed answer.
activities.intendedInsight: A worked before-and-after slide shows how each coordinate changed and reinforces that the shape keeps its size and orientation.

constraints: Built on first-quadrant coordinate knowledge; learners should already read ordered pairs along-then-up before describing moves as coordinate changes.

Recognition/selection responses (multiple-choice, tap-to-reveal) can be used while teaching and for scoring, but they do not require the learner to independently construct a predicted coordinate or a worded description — keep genuine prediction and production in the sequence.

The tap-to-reveal picture is a scaffold: because the slide is fixed, the learner cannot set, carry out or predict their own move; progress to an interactive or hand-plotted grid so the rule is used, not just read.

Count moves as unit jumps from the start point: do not count the starting line as 'one'; the first jump lands on the next line. (When points sit on grid intersections, counting square widths crossed gives the same count.) This avoids off-by-one images.
Keep directions and signs explicit: right/up add, left/down subtract; state them when working opposite directions.
Translations here are planar left/right/up/down slides; a 3D setting adds complexity irrelevant to this objective rather than being inherently unteachable in other media.

Self-audit of arithmetic/geometry: '4 right, 2 up' from (2,3) gives (6,5); (3,1) after '2 right, 3 up' gives (5,4); '2 left, 1 down' from (5,4) gives (3,3); (2,3)→(5,3) is '3 right' and reverses as '3 left'. The worked examples are internally consistent across summary, actions and feedback.

The original listed a reversal distractor producing '(4,7) or (6,5)' for '4 right, 2 up' from (2,3) — but (6,5) is the correct answer, so it cannot also be the swapped-components distractor; the genuinely swapped result is (4,7). probeDeeper: 'When the counter moved 3 to the right, why did only the first number change?' — listen for horizontal = x, height unchanged.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reversal — swaps the horizontal and vertical amounts, applying '4 right' to the y-coordinate and '2 up' to the x.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do the parts one at a time — right changes only x (first number), up only y (second) — tying the order back to along-then-up coordinates.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: After '4 right, 2 up' gives (4,7) or (6,5) with the components swapped; the image is in the wrong place along both axes.

errorPatterns.pattern: Changes the wrong coordinate — for a move described as 'right' alters the up-number, or changes both coordinates for a single-direction move.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show on the grid that a purely horizontal slide leaves the height (y) unchanged; label which number each direction affects before moving.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Moving (2,3) to the right yields a change in the second number, or both numbers change when only a horizontal move was asked.

errorPatterns.pattern: Counts squares not numbered lines — the image lands one line off, or the start of the count is misplaced.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Count the move on the numbered lines from the start position; no reteaching of translation needed — the count slipped.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: New coordinates are off by one; the child counts cells crossed rather than reading line labels from the start point.

errorPatterns.pattern: Confuses the move with the destination — when asked to DESCRIBE the move, states the end coordinates instead (or vice versa).
errorPatterns.nextMove: Distinguish the two questions explicitly — 'how did it move?' (units and direction) versus 'where is it now?' (coordinates); practise stating both for the same slide.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answers (1) with '(5,3)' rather than '3 right'; or when asked for the new position gives the shift amounts.

responseLevels.gap: Cannot describe or carry out a translation reliably: changes the wrong coordinate, reverses components, or the shape does not slide uniformly; predictions are guesses.
responseLevels.full: Describes moves precisely, carries out horizontal-and-vertical translations by adjusting x and y correctly, states the new coordinates, predicts an image without plotting, and knows the shape's size and orientation are unchanged — the (x+right, y+up) structure is applied, not just enacted.
responseLevels.partial: Describes and carries out a single-direction move (e.g. 3 right) correctly, but a two-part translation trips reversal or a wrong-coordinate change, or the child can only find the image by plotting rather than predicting from the rule — knows the pieces but doesn't combine them.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: On a first-quadrant grid, mark a point at (2,3). Say: (1) 'Move a counter from (2,3) to (5,3) — describe that move in words.' (2) 'Now translate this shape 4 units right and 2 units up; plot it and write the new coordinates of this corner.' (3) 'A point is at (3,1). Without plotting, tell me where it lands after moving 2 right and 3 up.' Watch how they handle each — do not prompt the rule.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The single-direction move (1) exposes children who change both coordinates or the wrong one; the two-part move (2) exposes reversal of the right/up amounts and non-uniform sliding; the predict item (3) separates children who can only move by counting on the grid from those who apply the (x+right, y+up) rule. pedagogy.summary: A coordinate pair names ONE location on a grid with an ORDERED pair of numbers: the first says how far to travel across from the origin (horizontal, the x-direction), the second how far up (vertical, the y-direction). The whole idea rests on two things children must hold together — that the order is a fixed convention (so (2,4) and (4,2) are different points), and that you read against the NUMBERED LINES from the origin (0,0), not by counting squares. The single most documented error is reversal: writing the vertical number before the horizontal. Taught well, coordinates are built on prior position language (along/across then up) and grounded in the physical act of travelling from the origin — 'along the corridor, then up the stairs' — before being abstracted to the (x, y) notation.
bestPractices: Fix the read as a two-step journey from the origin: ALONG first (how far across), THEN UP (how far up) — the 'along the corridor and up the stairs' image, with x = across (NCETM).
Make the order matter visibly: plot (2,4) and (4,2) on the same grid so children SEE they are different points, defeating the belief that order is arbitrary.
Read against the numbered LINES from the origin (0,0), not the squares — anchor counting at zero to avoid off-by-one errors.
Name the axes and connect names to coordinates (x-axis ↔ x-coordinate, first number; y-axis ↔ y-coordinate, second number), so reversal has a rule to fall back on ('x comes before y').
Move fluently between reading a plotted point and stating a shape's vertices, so a coordinate is seen as a location, not two loose numbers.
Build on Year 3/earlier position and direction vocabulary (left/right, up/down, across) before introducing the formal pair.
keyRepresentations: Numbered coordinate grid with the origin (0,0) marked
'Along the corridor, then up the stairs' journey from the origin (across before up)
Two contrasting points (2,4) vs (4,2) shown together to make order matter
The (x, y) ordered pair with axes labelled x (across) and y (up)
A shape plotted on the grid with each vertex's coordinates read off
commonMisconceptions: Reversal — putting the y-coordinate before the x (reading/plotting up before across), giving an incorrectly placed point (documented, NCETM).
Believing the order is arbitrary — treating (2,4) and (4,2) as the same location.
Counting squares/cells instead of reading the numbered grid lines, producing off-by-one positions.
Not anchoring to the origin — starting the count at 1 rather than 0, or from the wrong corner.

learn.summary: A coordinate pair names ONE location on a grid with an ORDERED pair of numbers: the first tells how far ACROSS from the origin (horizontal, x-direction), the second how far UP (vertical, y-direction). Two ideas must be held together: the order is a fixed convention (so (2,4) and (4,2) are different points), and you read against the NUMBERED LINES from the origin (0,0), not by counting the squares. The most documented error is reversal — writing the vertical number before the horizontal. Coordinates are well supported by prior position vocabulary (along/across, then up) and grounded in the physical image of travelling from the origin — 'along the corridor, then up the stairs' — before abstracting to (x, y) notation. Activities below range from an interactive place-and-see grid, through diagnostic reading tasks, to static reveal scaffolds; each has a distinct purpose and its own limits.

activities.title: Coordinate-journey grid: place the point and watch the path
feedback: When a placement is reversed, show the along-then-up trail and the target point together so the child sees it landed in a different place and why.
Use the compare mode to display (2,4) and (4,2) at once so 'order matters' is seen rather than told.
If the child starts counting at 1 or from the wrong corner, highlight the origin and the numbered line labels while re-counting from 0.
activities.rationale: Live tracing of the across-then-up journey and immediate placement feedback make the convention concrete, and plotting reversed pairs together surfaces the reversal and order-arbitrary misconceptions in the act of placing. Interaction such as path-tracing, the compare control, and glowing numbered lines are optional ways to make the mechanism visible, not required features.
sourceClaims: A common documented misconception is 'putting the y co-ordinate before the x, resulting in incorrectly placed position', caused by lack of knowledge of the order or of the names of the axes; suggested remedies include 'x comes before y' and 'along the corridor and up the stairs' (x is across). The Year 4 objective uses a grid where the lines are numbered, distinguishing reading numbered lines from counting squares.

A point in the plane is located by an ordered pair of numbers (its coordinates) measured from the origin along two perpendicular axes; the first number is travel along one axis and the second along the other, with the axis names and coordinate names corresponding (x-axis/x-coordinate, y-axis/y-coordinate); points are graphed in the first quadrant (5.G.1, 5.G.2).
learnerActions: Given a target pair such as (4,2), place the point on a numbered first-quadrant grid.
Watch the tool trace the journey from the origin — along 4, then up 2 — and drop the marker where you placed it.
If you read 'up before across', notice your point lands at 2-across-4-up, a clearly different point (a different gridline crossing) from the target (4,2), with the along-then-up trail showing why.
Press a compare control to drop (2,4) and (4,2) side by side so you SEE they are two different points.
Count against the glowing numbered lines starting from the origin (0,0), not the squares between them.
activities.intendedInsight: The order of the pair fixes the point — reading up before across lands you somewhere else — and counting is read from the numbered lines starting at the origin, not by counting squares.

activities.title: Read the point: diagnose reversal and off-by-one
feedback: If a child picks (4,2) for a point at 2-across-4-up, point out they read up before across and re-run the along-then-up read.
For an off-by-one answer such as (3,5) or (1,3) where (2,4) was intended, re-count against the numbered line labels from the origin, not the squares.
If a child names some vertices but not all, return to reading each corner as a single location.
activities.rationale: Reading a plotted point is cleanly scorable and the reversed pair makes a precise distractor that catches children who read up before across; an off-by-one option catches square-counting. This format is good for practice and diagnosis but, on its own, does not stage the place-and-watch-it-land-wrong moment — pair it with construction work. Recognising a correct option does not by itself show the child can independently construct a point.
sourceClaims: A common documented misconception is 'putting the y co-ordinate before the x, resulting in incorrectly placed position', caused by lack of knowledge of the order or of the names of the axes; suggested remedies include 'x comes before y' and 'along the corridor and up the stairs' (x is across). The Year 4 objective uses a grid where the lines are numbered, distinguishing reading numbered lines from counting squares.

A point in the plane is located by an ordered pair of numbers (its coordinates) measured from the origin along two perpendicular axes; the first number is travel along one axis and the second along the other, with the axis names and coordinate names corresponding (x-axis/x-coordinate, y-axis/y-coordinate); points are graphed in the first quadrant (5.G.1, 5.G.2).
learnerActions: Read the coordinates of a plotted point on a numbered grid and write them as an ordered pair, e.g. (3,5).
Answer 'which of these is (2,4)?' with (4,2) also offered, choosing the correct point.
Match and name the coordinates of all vertices of a plotted shape.
Explain which number is 'across' and which is 'up' for each answer.
activities.intendedInsight: Reading a plotted point as (across, up) can be checked reliably, and a reversed or off-by-one answer indicates which misconception is likely at work.

activities.title: Labelled-grid reveal: seed the convention and the axis names
feedback: When a reading is revealed, restate it as across-first, up-second so the order is reinforced.
Tie the first number to the x-axis by name so reversal has a rule to correct it.
activities.rationale: Connecting axis names to coordinate names and surfacing the across-first reading seeds the convention and supports recall of the order; the 'x comes before y' mnemonic is a documented remedy for reversal. This is a seeding/reference scaffold: it presents fixed examples to read and name, so on its own it does not let the child test a placement or experience order mattering through their own action — follow it with construction and reading tasks.

The Year 4 objective uses a grid where the lines are numbered, distinguishing reading numbered lines from counting squares.

A point in the plane is located by an ordered pair of numbers (its coordinates) measured from the origin along two perpendicular axes; the first number is travel along one axis and the second along the other, with the axis names and coordinate names corresponding (x-axis/x-coordinate, y-axis/y-coordinate); points are graphed in the first quadrant (5.G.1, 5.G.2).
learnerActions: Tap a point on a labelled grid to reveal its along-then-up reading (across first, then up).
Tap the x- and y-axes to reveal 'x = across, first number' and 'y = up, second number'.
Lift a flap comparing (2,4) and (4,2) to see they name different points.
Say aloud the rule 'x comes before y' and connect each axis name to its coordinate.
activities.intendedInsight: Each number in the pair has a fixed meaning tied to a named axis, giving a rule ('x comes before y') to fall back on when unsure of the order.

activities.title: Name the corners: coordinates as locations of a shape
feedback: If a vertex is reversed, re-run the along-then-up read for that corner.
For the (0,3) case, confirm a zero across is still a valid coordinate read from the origin.
If a child says A and B are the same, plot both and show the two distinct points (A at (2,4), B at (4,2)).
activities.rationale: Reading vertices and probing the origin and zero-coordinate cases tests coordinates as locations across several points and forces the order-matters distinction. Aligned to the topic evidence of reading points, explaining horizontal/vertical, and identifying all vertices of a plotted shape.
sourceClaims: A point in the plane is located by an ordered pair of numbers (its coordinates) measured from the origin along two perpendicular axes; the first number is travel along one axis and the second along the other, with the axis names and coordinate names corresponding (x-axis/x-coordinate, y-axis/y-coordinate); points are graphed in the first quadrant (5.G.1, 5.G.2).
learnerActions: Read aloud the coordinates of every corner of a rectangle (or other shape) plotted on the grid.
Decide whether a point sitting on the up-line at height 3 with nothing across is (0,3).
Judge a claim such as 'B was written as (2,4), the same as A' when the grid shows A at 2-across-4-up and B at 4-across-2-up — show on the grid why it is right or wrong.
Explain how you remember which number comes first.
activities.intendedInsight: A coordinate is a single location, not two loose numbers; moving between a plotted point, a vertex, and the origin consolidates reading and justifies the order.

constraints: Scope is the first quadrant with a numbered grid for ages 8–9; whole-number coordinates read from the origin (0,0).

The static labelled-grid reveal seeds the convention and axis names but does not let a child test a placement or experience order mattering through their own action; use it alongside construction and reading tasks, not as the sole experience.
Reading/selected-response items diagnose and give practice but do not by themselves elicit independent construction of a point; pair them with place-the-point work.
Build on Year 3/earlier position vocabulary (left/right, up/down, across) before introducing the formal (x, y) pair.
Counting must be anchored at the origin and read against the numbered lines, not the squares between them, to avoid off-by-one errors.

Interaction examples (path tracing, compare control, glowing numbered lines, tap-to-reveal, lift-the-flap) are optional ways to make the mechanism concrete and should not be treated as mandatory mechanisms.
