probeDeeper: 'Point to (0,0). If a point sits right on the up-line at height 3, what are its coordinates?' — checks the origin anchor and a zero x-coordinate.
Counterexample: 'A friend wrote B as (2,4), the same as A. Is that right? Show me on the grid why or why not.' — forces the order-matters distinction.
'Which number tells you how far across, and which tells you how far up? How do you remember which comes first?' — surfaces the rule versus a guess.
'Read me the coordinates of every corner of this rectangle' — tests reading a coordinate as a location across several vertices.
assess.correctAnswer: A = (2,4), B = (4,2). The first number is how far ACROSS (horizontal, x) and the second is how far UP (vertical, y), counted from the origin (0,0); A and B are DIFFERENT points because the order matters.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reversal — reads/writes the vertical number before the horizontal ('up before across'), so A is given as (4,2) and B as (2,4).
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reinstate 'along the corridor, then up the stairs' (x = across, first); tie the first number to the x-axis by name; practise placing a point and checking the along-then-up path.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: A and B are swapped; or the child counts up first then across; justification appeals to no rule about which axis is first.

errorPatterns.pattern: Order treated as arbitrary — says (2,4) and (4,2) name the same point, so A and B are 'the same'.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Plot (2,4) and (4,2) together so the two different squares are seen; stress that a coordinate is an ORDERED pair — the order fixes the point.
errorPatterns.distractor: A and B are the same point
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Claims A and B are the same location, or that swapping the numbers makes no difference; may write the pairs correctly but see no distinction.

errorPatterns.pattern: Counts squares instead of the numbered lines — reads off-by-one, or starts counting from 1 rather than the origin.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Anchor counting at the origin (0,0) and read the NUMBERED lines, not the squares between them; point to the line labels while counting.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Gives A as (3,5) or (1,3); counts the cells crossed rather than reading the line labels; does not start at 0.

responseLevels.gap: Cannot reliably read a point's coordinates: reverses, counts squares, or cannot say which number comes first; no notion that order fixes the point.
responseLevels.full: Reads any first-quadrant point as (across, up) from the origin, explains the first number is horizontal (x) and the second vertical (y), knows (2,4)≠(4,2), and reads off all the vertices of a plotted shape correctly.
responseLevels.partial: Reads a point correctly in a clear case and knows the pair has two numbers, but reverses when the two values are confusable, or reads correctly yet cannot justify the order (treats it as arbitrary), or is off-by-one from counting squares — cannot yet read all of a shape's vertices dependably.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Show a first-quadrant grid with numbered lines. Plot two points: A at 2 across and 4 up, B at 4 across and 2 up. Ask: 'Write the coordinates of A and of B.' Then: 'How do you decide which number to write first — and are A and B the same point or different?'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Two points that are coordinate-reversals of each other mean a child who reverses x and y will swap A and B — the error is unmissable. The second tier separates a child who happened to write the right pair from one who understands WHY: a child who says 'the order doesn't matter' or 'you go up first' reveals the misconception even if one label came out right. A correct answer for the right reason names across-then-up from the origin.

topic.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is playing a game where ships can be at negative coordinates too, can they correctly plot and read positions like (−3, 2) or (1, −4) on a grid?

pedagogy.summary: Children extend coordinate work to the full plane: plotting and reading points such as (−3,4) and (2,−5) across all four quadrants, naming which quadrant a point lies in, and describing positions where either or both coordinates are negative. The new demand is not the (across, up) convention itself — that carries over from the first quadrant — but reading a SIGNED scale on each axis: a negative x means left of the origin, a negative y means below it, and the numbers run symmetrically outward from 0 in both directions. Success rests on secure directed-number sense fused to the ordered-pair rule.
bestPractices: Anchor both axes as signed number lines meeting at the origin: rehearse pointing and chanting positive and negative values on a counting stick held horizontally (x) and vertically (y), forwards and backwards, so left/below map to negatives (NCETM).
Emphasise the symmetry about 0 — the numbers mirror outward from the origin — so children read −3 as three to the LEFT, not three to the right.
Keep the reading rule explicit and mnemonic — 'along the corridor and up (or down) the stairs', 'x is a-cross', 'x before y' — to hold off the perennial y-before-x reversal (NCETM).
Always plot the first coordinate along x from the origin THEN the second along y, treating each sign as a direction, not a decoration on the digit.
Name the four quadrants by the sign pattern of their points (+,+), (−,+), (−,−), (+,−) so 'which quadrant?' becomes a reading of the two signs, and connect this to reflections in the axes.
Use problems that force reasoning across quadrants (find the fourth vertex of a square given (3,0), (0,3), (−3,0)) rather than isolated plotting, so signs must be coordinated.
keyRepresentations: Four-quadrant coordinate grid with the origin and both signed axes labelled
Counting stick / number line held horizontally and vertically to model signed movement along each axis
Thermometer or below-ground scale as a familiar signed vertical axis
Sign-pattern labels for the four quadrants: (+,+), (−,+), (−,−), (+,−)
commonMisconceptions: Moving the wrong way for a negative coordinate — counting right for −3 or up for −5 — through weak grasp of order on a signed scale.
Putting the y-coordinate before the x-coordinate, placing the point in the wrong quadrant.
Mis-ordering negatives (treating −5 as further out than −3 because 5>3), so points on a negative axis are misplaced.
Counting from '1' at the origin instead of '0', landing one square off.

learn.summary: Children extend coordinate work to all four quadrants: plotting and reading points such as (−3,4) and (2,−5), naming which quadrant a point lies in, and reasoning about positions where either or both coordinates are negative. The new demand is reading a SIGNED scale on each axis — a negative x means left of the origin, a negative y means below it, with numbers running symmetrically outward from 0 — fused to the ordered-pair (across, then up/down) rule. Live plotting with immediate feedback lets wrong-direction and reversed placements surface and be corrected; discrete practice items and labelled grids can check and clarify but elicit less of the felt signed movement.

activities.title: Plot it as a signed journey from the origin
feedback: If (−3,4) lands in the top-right (first) quadrant, the x-move went the wrong way: count the negative as LEFT from 0 and re-plot.
If the point lands as if it were (4,−3), the pair was reversed — move along x first ('along the corridor, then up or down the stairs').
Linked feedback that lights each axis's signed count as the marker travels makes the two moves and the landing quadrant visible together.
Reflecting (−3,4) in the x-axis gives (−3,−4) — the y-sign flips and the point drops to the third quadrant; check which single sign changed.
activities.rationale: Plotting on a signed grid is direct manipulation: the child performs two signed movements and can see a wrong direction or a reversed pair immediately, which is where signed-coordinate errors surface. Reading the quadrant from the sign pattern and linking sign flips to reflection connects the skill to geometry the child already knows.

Recommended teaching includes mnemonics ('along the corridor and up the stairs', 'x is a-cross', 'x before y'), chanting positive and negative numbers on a counting stick held both horizontally and vertically for the two axes, and referring to the symmetry of the numbers about 0.
learnerActions: On a four-quadrant grid with a labelled origin and signed axes, plot (−3,4): move LEFT 3 along the x-axis from the origin, then UP 4 along the y-axis, treating each sign as a direction.
Name the quadrant from its sign pattern: (−,+) is the second (top-left) quadrant.
Plot (2,−5) (two right, five down) and (−4,−1) (four left, one down), naming each quadrant from its two signs.

If a live tool is available, place the marker yourself and watch it replay the two signed moves; if you counted right for the −3 and landed in the (+,+) quadrant, notice the mismatch and re-plot reading the minus as 'left'.
Where offered, use a reflect-in-axis toggle to flip (−3,4)↔(3,4)↔(3,−4) and watch a single sign change hop the point across an axis.
activities.intendedInsight: A minus sign is a DIRECTION (left of, or below, the origin), not decoration on the digit; the quadrant is read directly from the pair of signs, and flipping one sign reflects the point across an axis.

activities.title: Anchor each axis as a signed number line
feedback: If the child taps the origin while saying 'one', re-establish the origin as 0 and count moves from there; otherwise every point lands one square off.
If −5 is placed nearer the origin than −3 because 5>3, count steps out from 0 on the line: −5 is five steps out, −3 is three.
A counting stick or washing-line chanted in both directions makes the symmetry about 0 audible and visible.
activities.rationale: Secure directed-number sense underpins signed plotting; ordering negatives is genuinely hard because children treat magnitude as value, and number-line / thermometer / depth models address this by foregrounding position on the scale.
sourceClaims: Children find ordering negative integers difficult — numbers less than zero represent 'the non-existent' and the idea that 0 is greater than −1 is hard; the underlying error is treating the magnitude/digit as the value rather than the position on the scale, best addressed with number-line, washing-line, thermometer and swimming-pool (depth) models.

learnerActions: Treat the x-axis as a horizontal number line and the y-axis as a vertical one, both meeting at 0 at the origin.
Point and chant positive and negative values along a counting stick held horizontally, then vertically, forwards and backwards, so left and below map to negatives.

pedagogy.summary: The coordinate system is built from two perpendicular NUMBER LINES — the x-axis (horizontal) and the y-axis (vertical) — crossing at the origin (0,0). An ordered pair (x, y) names ONE unique point by two distances from the origin: the first number is how far ALONG the x-axis (horizontal), the second how far UP the y-axis (vertical). The order is a convention that carries meaning, so (2,4) and (4,2) are different points. The dominant error is reversal — reading or writing the pair in the wrong order (y before x, 'up before across'); a second is treating the axes as blank space rather than number lines, so the child counts squares instead of reading the numbered lines and/or loses the origin as the (0,0) anchor.
bestPractices: Build the axes as two number lines the child already knows, laid perpendicular and meeting at 0 (the origin); a point's coordinates are just readings on those two number lines
Fix the order with a memorable rule — 'x is a-cross, then up', 'along the corridor, then up the stairs', x before y — and always read horizontal first
Contrast (2,4) with (4,2) explicitly so the child sees that changing the order changes the point
Read from the numbered LINES, not by counting squares, and anchor every reading at the origin (0,0)
Name and point to the x-axis, y-axis and origin repeatedly so the vocabulary is secure
keyRepresentations: Two perpendicular number lines meeting at the origin, each labelled; the point reached by reading along then up
The 'corridor then stairs' / 'a-cross then up' journey traced from the origin to the point
(2,4) and (4,2) plotted together to show the order matters
A grid with numbered lines (not just squares) to read off directly
commonMisconceptions: Reversal — gives/reads the pair as (y, x): up before across (NCETM: 'putting the y-coordinate before the x')
Treats order as arbitrary — thinks (2,4) and (4,2) are the same point
Counts squares/gaps from the edge instead of reading the numbered lines from the origin (off-by-one)
Loses the origin as the (0,0) start, or thinks the axes are just the borders of the grid rather than number lines

learn.summary: Teach the coordinate pair as an ORDERED address read off two perpendicular number lines (x-axis horizontal, y-axis vertical) that meet at the origin (0,0). The first number is distance ALONG the x-axis, the second is distance UP the y-axis, so (2,4) and (4,2) are different points. Target the two dominant errors: reversal (writing/reading y before x) and counting squares from a grid edge instead of reading the numbered lines from the origin. Core activities use a plotting/journey task where swapping the same two numbers lands on different points; alternatives include a labelled reference grid and a navigator-talk task that each serve a narrower purpose.

Read the numbered LINES, not the squares: start at 0 (the origin) and find the line by READING its printed label — the line labelled 4 is the one printed with a 4 — rather than counting squares or gaps from the edge.
If you reversed a pair, re-trace from the origin saying the first number aloud as the across move.
activities.rationale: Plotting both reversed pairs and seeing them land on different points is intended to target the reversal error and the 'order is arbitrary' misconception; starting every journey from the origin and reading numbered lines targets the count-squares/off-by-one error. Fixing the order with a stated mnemonic is a commonly used remedy.

pedagogy.summary: Plotting and reading ordered pairs in the first quadrant is a procedure built on the coordinate-system convention (x before y, both measured from the origin). Best taught by first securing the convention as a rule of movement — 'along the corridor, then up the stairs' — then having children plot given pairs, read back plotted points, and crucially graph real data pairs (e.g. time vs distance) so a coordinate stops being an abstract dot and becomes a meaningful statement about a situation. The interpret-in-context step (evidence bullet 3) is what separates fluent plotting from mechanical dot-placement.
bestPractices: Rehearse the x-before-y convention as a fixed sequence of movements from the origin ('across, then up') before any data work, so the ordered pair is read as a route, not two loose numbers
Insist children count along the numbered lines/gridlines, not the squares between them, to pre-empt the off-by-one error
Move quickly from plotting bare pairs to graphing real data pairs (time vs distance, cost vs quantity) and asking 'what does this point tell us?' so coordinates carry meaning
Use grids whose axes are scaled in steps other than one (twos, fives) once the basic convention is secure, so children read the scale rather than assuming one-square-equals-one
Have children both plot (given the pair, mark the point) and read (given the point, state the pair) in the same session — the two directions expose different errors
keyRepresentations: First-quadrant coordinate grid with clearly numbered axes and a marked origin
'Corridor then stairs' / 'along then up' movement metaphor for the x-then-y order
Data table paired with its plotted graph (e.g. time in column 1, distance in column 2) so each row becomes a point
Journey/time-distance line built from plotted points, linking each dot to a moment in a story

learn.summary: Plotting and reading ordered pairs in the first quadrant is a procedure built on the coordinate convention: x before y, both counted from the origin along numbered gridlines. Secure the convention as a fixed rule of movement ('along the corridor, then up the stairs'), have children both plot given pairs and read plotted points back, then graph real data pairs (e.g. time vs distance) so each coordinate becomes a meaningful statement about a situation rather than a bare dot. Interpreting a point in context is part of the objective, not an add-on, and is what separates fluent plotting from mechanical dot-placement.

activities.title: Plot a journey: the snail's progress
feedback: If the point lands as a mirror image across the diagonal, the pair has been reversed — re-narrate 'along before up, x always first' and re-place it

If a point sits one place short or beyond, the child has probably miscounted, for example by counting the origin line as 1 or by counting squares rather than numbered lines — put a finger on the origin and count the numbered lines aloud, touching each number, noting the numbers label the lines not the spaces

If the child places the point correctly but says 'it's just the point', read the axes aloud together ('this way is minutes, this way is centimetres') and ask them to finish 'after ___ minutes the snail had gone ___'
activities.rationale: Graphing real data pairs and interpreting them in context is an explicit part of the fifth-grade standard; the ordered pair (x,y) gives horizontal then vertical distance from the origin.

learnerActions: On a numbered first-quadrant grid, plot the ordered pairs (1,2), (2,4), (3,6) for a snail logging its distance each minute, marking each point at the intersection of the numbered gridlines
Narrate the route aloud while plotting: 'along the corridor to 3, then up the stairs to 6'
After plotting (3,6), answer 'what does this point tell us?' by completing the sentence 'after 3 minutes the snail had gone 6 centimetres'
Join the plotted points to see the journey line emerge
activities.intendedInsight: A coordinate is not just a dot: it is a two-number route from the origin (x first, then y) and, on a data graph, a statement about a real situation.

activities.title: Read it back: from point to pair to meaning
feedback: If the child reads (5,8) as (8,5), the pair has been reversed — reinforce x first by counting along before up
If the child claims (7,4) and (4,7) are the same point, have both marked at once so the mismatch is visible and the order is forced to matter
activities.rationale: Plotting and reading in the same session exposes different errors; pupils commonly reverse coordinates, so explicitly contrasting (a,b) with (b,a) targets that misconception.
sourceClaims: Pupils commonly reverse coordinates (plotting y before x / 'up before across') and count squares rather than the numbered gridlines when reading and plotting points
learnerActions: On a new graph for a different journey — a car this time — read the marked point at (5,8), stating its coordinates by counting along then up from the origin
Say what the point means in the car's journey: 'after 5 minutes the car had gone 8 km'
Compare (7,4) and (4,7) by plotting both, confirming they are different points, so the order of the pair matters
activities.intendedInsight: Reading a plotted point reverses the plotting procedure and exposes different errors; order is not interchangeable because (a,b) and (b,a) are different points whenever a and b differ.

activities.title: Read the scale, don't count squares
feedback: If a point lands at the wrong height on the twos-scaled axis, the child has counted squares — point to the printed axis numbers and ask 'what number is this line?' before replacing the point
Practise on grids scaled in twos and fives, reading a value before plotting each time
activities.rationale: Introducing non-unit scales once the basic convention is secure pre-empts the assumption that one square equals one unit and makes children read the numbered axis.
learnerActions: Work on a grid whose vertical axis is numbered 0,2,4,6,8,10 in twos while the horizontal is in ones
Before plotting a value, read aloud the number printed on the target gridline ('what number is this line?')
Plot a point that 'looks like 4 squares up' but is actually at 8 on the twos-scaled axis, reading the printed number rather than counting squares
activities.intendedInsight: One square does not always equal one unit; the numbers printed on the axis determine position, so the scale must be read before plotting.

activities.title: Predict the next point
feedback: If the child can only place given dots but not predict, draw attention to how the distance changes with each extra minute in the table (it goes up by 2 each time)
If the child treats (0,0) as meaningless, prompt: at 0 minutes the snail has travelled 0 centimetres — the starting point of the journey
activities.rationale: Reading the data relationship and interpreting coordinate values in context, including the origin, extends plotting beyond mechanical dot-placement as required by the standard.
sourceClaims: Fifth-grade coordinate work is to 'represent real world and mathematical problems by graphing points in the first quadrant' and 'interpret coordinate values of points in the context of the situation' — the interpret-in-context step is part of the standard, not an add-on
learnerActions: Given the snail's plotted pattern (1,2), (2,4), (3,6), work out where the point for 4 minutes would go if the pattern continued, and plot it at (4,8)
Explain the relationship in the data table (distance = 2 x minutes) that lets you predict the un-plotted point
Interpret the origin (0,0) in context: what does it mean about the snail at time zero?
activities.intendedInsight: A graph of data pairs encodes a relationship, so points can be predicted, not just copied from a table; the origin itself carries meaning in context.

constraints: Count along the numbered gridlines, not the squares between them, to pre-empt the off-by-one error; make explicit that the numbers label the lines, not the spaces
Rehearse the x-before-y convention as a fixed sequence of movements from the origin ('across, then up') before any data work, so the ordered pair is read as a route rather than two loose numbers
Introduce non-unit axis scales (twos, fives) only once the basic convention is secure
Children should both plot (mark the point from a pair) and read (state the pair from a point) in the same session — the two directions expose different errors

Keep each activity's real-data scenario internally consistent (same object and same distance unit throughout a single activity) so a coordinate reliably maps to one situation; where the object changes between activities, frame the new journey explicitly

Recognition-only or recall tasks (e.g. selecting the right pair from options) assess the plot/read skill but do not elicit the independent construction of plotting a point or an open explanation of what a coordinate means; include tasks that require actually placing points and stating meaning in a child's own words

A tap-to-reveal static grid can introduce the convention (e.g. tap a point to reveal 'across 4, up 7') but does not let the child perform a placement or receive feedback on their own plotting; treat it as a pre-teach scaffold, not practice of the skill
The skill is planar (two axes in a flat plane); a third dimension is not part of this objective

Interactive grid examples (snapping a placed point to the gridline intersection, a growing journey line, a data-table row lighting up its point, live confirmation of a placement) are optional ways to make the mechanism concrete, not required features
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source lists National Curriculum (England) Year 6 as verified:false; treat that claim as unconfirmed. The two Common Core 5.G claims and the NCETM misconceptions claim are marked verified in the source but have not been re-checked here.

Arithmetic and ordering are consistent: (1,2),(2,4),(3,6) follow distance = 2 x minutes, so a 4-minute point at (4,8) is a valid prediction and (0,0) is the snail's starting point; (5,8) reads as 5 along, 8 up.

The guidance uses two separate real-data scenarios across activities — a snail measured in metres (Activities 1, 3, 4) and a car measured in km (Activity 2). The split is inherited from the original (snail in the recommendation, car in the assessment) and is deliberate because (5,8) does not fit the snail's distance = 2 x minutes pattern (its 5-minute point is (5,10)). Activity 2 now frames the car as a different journey so the object change is explicit; a single learner path could instead be unified by substituting a read-back point consistent with the snail's pattern.

The original row framed conversation and 3D formats as having no value; this has been reframed in constraints as scope limits (the skill is planar; talk about coordinates differs from performing the procedure) rather than universal claims about those media.

'This point is at (0,0) — what does that mean about the car?' — probing whether the origin carries meaning in context

topic.assessmentPrompt: If you show {{name}} half a shape drawn on squared paper with a mirror line marked, can they draw the missing half so the whole shape is perfectly symmetrical?

pedagogy.summary: Children complete the missing half of a symmetric figure across a given mirror line — finishing a butterfly, a pattern on squared paper, or a shape — and verify it by folding. The skill is applied reflection: every point of the drawn half has a partner the same perpendicular distance on the other side of the mirror, and joining these partners reconstructs the whole. Done well it is point-by-point and checkable by folding; done poorly it is a freehand 'looks about right' sketch. The fold test is both the method's justification and its self-check.
bestPractices: Complete the figure point by point, not by eye: for each corner or key point of the given half, count the squares perpendicular to the mirror line, then count the same number on the far side and mark the partner point; join the partners in the same order.
Insist every partner point is EQUIDISTANT from the mirror line — the reflected feature is the same distance out, not roughly opposite; use the squared grid to count exactly.
Make sure the completed half is a mirror image (sense reversed), not a slid copy — a butterfly's second wing points the opposite way; contrast reflecting with translating.
Handle points that sit ON the mirror line explicitly: they stay put (distance zero), so they are not duplicated or shifted.
Always check by folding along the mirror line so the two halves coincide (or use a mirror/Mira on the line); this both proves correctness and defines what symmetry means (NCETM).
Progress from patterns and vertical mirrors to horizontal and, later, sloping mirror lines, keeping the 'perpendicular and equidistant' rule constant so it generalises (NCETM KS3 6.3).
keyRepresentations: Squared grid with a marked mirror line and the given half of the figure
Perpendicular counting arrows from each point of the given half to its partner on the far side
Fold test / Mira mirror placed on the line to verify the halves coincide
Butterfly or letter half as an intuitive 'complete the other side' context
commonMisconceptions: Completing the figure by eye so the reflected points are not equidistant from the mirror line.
Sliding a copy of the half across (translating) rather than reflecting, so the completed shape is not a true mirror image.
Miscounting the squares, so individual partner points land the wrong distance from the mirror.
Duplicating or shifting points that lie on the mirror line instead of leaving them fixed.

learn.summary: Children complete the missing half of a symmetric figure across a given mirror line (a butterfly, a pattern on squared paper, or a shape) point by point, and verify by folding along the line so the halves coincide. The core idea: every point of the drawn half has a partner the same perpendicular distance on the other side of the mirror; joining these partners in the same order reconstructs the whole as a true mirror image (sense reversed, not a slid copy). The fold test is both the construction method's justification and its self-check. Progress from vertical to horizontal and later sloping mirror lines, holding the 'perpendicular and equidistant' rule constant.

activities.title: Build the butterfly's missing wing, point by point
feedback: If the second half is sketched freehand and roughly opposite, return to counting squares: the reflected feature must be the SAME distance out, not approximately mirrored. Then fold to confirm.
If one or two points are a square off, don't reteach reflection — just re-count that point, mark the equal perpendicular squares on both sides, and fold to self-correct.

If the completed half folds onto the original everywhere (allowing for small folding inaccuracies), that is good evidence the figure is symmetric; the equal square-counts on both sides are what justify it.
activities.rationale: Completing a symmetric figure is itself a point-by-point reflection with an immediate fold check; doing it by hand on a grid with physical folding makes the perpendicular-equidistant relationship concrete and gives a built-in verification. The curriculum expects Year 4 pupils to complete a simple symmetric figure about a specific line of symmetry.
sourceClaims: Reflection sends each point perpendicular to the mirror line to an equal distance on the far side (the mirror line is the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining a point to its image); teaching should avoid 'straight across' language so the rule generalises to sloping mirrors.

Suggested symmetry activities include completing half a symmetrical shape using the line of symmetry and checking by drawing round, cutting out and folding so the halves coincide (careless cutting can affect results).
Year 4 pupils should complete a simple symmetric figure with respect to a specific line of symmetry.
learnerActions: Start from half a butterfly drawn on squared paper beside a clearly marked vertical mirror line.
For each key point of the given half (e.g. a wingtip), count the squares perpendicular from the mirror line to that point.
Count the SAME number of squares straight out on the far side, perpendicular to the mirror, and mark the partner point.
Repeat for every corner/key point, then join the partners in the SAME order as the original half.

Fold the paper along the mirror line (holding it up to the light if needed), or stand a mirror/Mira on the line and compare the reflection of the given half with your drawn half. Check that the two halves line up, allowing for small inaccuracies in drawing and folding.
If the fold misses anywhere, find the slipped point, re-count its squares on both sides, and correct it.
activities.intendedInsight: Reflection sends each point perpendicular to the mirror line to an equal distance on the far side; building partner-by-partner (counting equal perpendicular distances) and folding to check turns a 'looks about right' sketch into a construction you can justify and check.

activities.title: Reflect, don't slide: spot the difference
feedback: If a learner accepts the slid copy as symmetric, point to the two wings pointing the SAME way, then fold: the halves fail to coincide, so it is not a reflection.
Contrast the words: 'reflect' flips the sense; 'slide' keeps it. Rebuild one feature by the perpendicular-equidistant rule to see the reversal emerge.
activities.rationale: A classic error is translating rather than reflecting; explicitly contrasting the two, with a fold test as arbiter, targets the sense-reversal property directly.
sourceClaims: Reflection uniquely reverses 'sense', distinguishing a true mirror image from a shape merely slid (translated) across.

Suggested symmetry activities include completing half a symmetrical shape using the line of symmetry and checking by drawing round, cutting out and folding so the halves coincide (careless cutting can affect results).
learnerActions: Look at two completions of the same half-butterfly: one where the second wing points the opposite way, one where a copy of the left wing has been slid across so both wings point the same way.
Decide which is truly symmetric and explain how you can tell.
Fold each along the mirror line and watch which one's halves coincide.
Say what folding reveals about the slid copy (the wingtips miss).
activities.intendedInsight: Reflection reverses 'sense' — a true mirror image faces the opposite way, unlike a shape merely slid (translated) across, which keeps the same orientation and, for a lopsided half like a butterfly wing, will not fold onto the original half.

activities.title: Points on the line, and new mirror directions
feedback: If a learner duplicates or shifts an on-the-line point, note its distance from the line is zero, so its partner is itself.
If horizontal or sloping mirrors cause trouble, re-state the rule as 'perpendicular to the mirror, equal distance' rather than 'straight across', so it transfers to any direction.
A fold that fails for a sloping mirror helps show where a partner point was misplaced, so you can re-count that point's perpendicular distance.
activities.rationale: Avoiding 'straight across' language and handling on-the-line points explicitly lets the rule generalise beyond vertical mirrors, which the misconception list flags as a common failure point.
sourceClaims: Reflection sends each point perpendicular to the mirror line to an equal distance on the far side (the mirror line is the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining a point to its image); teaching should avoid 'straight across' language so the rule generalises to sloping mirrors.
learnerActions: Work a figure that has a key point sitting right ON the mirror line; decide where its partner goes (it stays put — distance zero, not duplicated or shifted).
Complete a figure whose mirror line is HORIZONTAL, counting squares perpendicular to that line (now up/down).

Later, try a figure with a SLOPING mirror line (on squared paper, a diagonal line at 45°), keeping the same rule: each partner the same perpendicular distance from the line, counted in corner-to-corner diagonal steps across the squares.
Fold (or imagine the fold) along each mirror line to check the halves coincide.
activities.intendedInsight: The 'perpendicular and equidistant' rule is constant whatever the mirror's orientation; points on the line are fixed, and the method generalises from vertical to horizontal and sloping lines.

activities.title: Check and choose: deciding if a completion is correct
feedback: If you choose the slid (same-orientation) copy, notice both halves face the SAME way, so it cannot be a reflection; fold it and the wingtips miss.
If you choose the version with a point one square off, re-count that point's perpendicular distance from the mirror on both sides; a fold would fail just at that point.

Recognising correct completions and predicting whether a fold would match confirm your understanding, but they do not by themselves make you build and fold your own figure, so pair them with at least one hands-on completion.
activities.rationale: Recognition and fold-prediction questions are efficient for checking whether learners can distinguish correct reflections from the two characteristic errors, provided they complement rather than replace construction-and-fold work.
sourceClaims: Reflection uniquely reverses 'sense', distinguishing a true mirror image from a shape merely slid (translated) across.
learnerActions: On a grid, complete a given half by marking the partner points and joining them.
From several completed figures, pick the correctly reflected one, rejecting a wrong version that is the half slid across (same orientation) and another where a point is one square off.
Decide whether folding a figure along the mirror line would make the halves match, and say yes or no.
Justify each choice by counting squares or by predicting the fold.
activities.intendedInsight: Being able to recognise correct reflections — and name exactly why the slid-copy and one-square-off versions are wrong — consolidates the perpendicular-equidistant and sense-reversal rules.

constraints: The task should require the learner to construct and fold-check their OWN figure; recognition-only questions (pick the right completion, or judge whether a fold would match) confirm discrimination but do not elicit independent construction of a symmetric figure.

A static or tap-to-reveal worked example (showing each partner point's square-count and a fold overlay) can demonstrate the method, but on its own does not let the learner complete and fold-test their own figure, which is the skill; use it as a scaffold, not the whole task.
Keep the language 'perpendicular to the mirror, equal distance' rather than 'straight across', so the rule transfers to horizontal and sloping mirror lines.
Handle on-the-line points explicitly: they are fixed (distance zero), not duplicated or shifted.
Paper cutouts and folds have real thickness and careless cutting/folding can affect results; treat the fold as an approximate physical check of an ideal reflection.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source rated planar (2D) construction the best fit and marked 3D and conversation formats 'poor' with claims that 3D 'distracts' and a character 'cannot supply' plotting/fold verification. These are scoped as 'this planar grid task fits 2D construction best'; they are not universal laws. A discussion could still support reasoning, and a physical/tactile fold is one effective check among others — not claimed as the only way.

The source's framing that only live/interactive manipulation turns a guess into a tested construction has been softened: physical paper-and-fold work achieves the same construct-and-check loop; interactive recolouring/snapping are optional aids, not the only mechanism.
The Year 4 National Curriculum claim is marked verified:false in the source; it is retained (including in activity 1 sourceClaims) as stated but remains unverified.

An author-facing instruction in the check-and-choose activity ('design a wrong option so...') was rewritten as learner-facing feedback, and question-format jargon was removed from learner-facing text.

topic.description: Represent and carry out geometric transformations on squared paper or a coordinate grid: reflections (in horizontal, vertical, and diagonal mirror lines, including the axes), translations (described as a vector or as left/right/up/down moves), and rotations (90° or 180° about a stated centre point); describe each transformation precisely using the correct language; identify which transformation maps one shape onto its image by comparing position, orientation, and size
evidence: Reflect a shape in a given mirror line on a grid and label the new coordinates
Translate a shape by a given number of squares horizontally and vertically and describe the movement
Rotate a shape 90° or 180° about a given centre on a grid and check the image is congruent to the original
topic.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees a shape and its mirror image on squared paper, can they draw in the exact mirror line, and describe the reflection precisely — including where the line of reflection is — without just saying 'it flipped'?

pedagogy.summary: This is the representational core of transformations: reading a picture of an object and its image and saying precisely WHICH transformation maps one onto the other — and, conversely, producing the image from a described transformation. Each transformation has a defining set of marks a child must read and generate: a reflection needs a mirror line (and reverses sense); a translation needs a vector/displacement (and keeps orientation and sense); a rotation needs three things — a centre, an angle of turn, and a direction. Fluency means translating freely between the drawn image and its precise verbal description, checking congruence throughout.
bestPractices: Teach each transformation by its distinguishing evidence: reflection is the only one that reverses 'sense' (handedness); rotation changes orientation but keeps sense; translation keeps both. Have children CHECK sense to tell rotation from reflection.
Insist a rotation is described by all THREE pieces — centre of rotation, size of turn, and direction (clockwise/anticlockwise); a description missing any one is incomplete (NCETM KS3 6.3).

For reflection, draw the perpendicular lines joining each object vertex to its image and show the mirror line is their perpendicular bisector; avoid 'straight across/down' so the idea survives sloping mirror lines.
Move both ways: given an image, have the child NAME and fully describe the transformation; given a description, have the child PRODUCE the image — the two directions reinforce each other.
Use tracing paper for rotation — pin the centre, turn to the stated angle and direction — so the abstract description becomes a felt movement, and to verify congruence.

Include non-standard cases (a rotation that could be read clockwise or anticlockwise; a reflection in a sloping line) to force analysis rather than pattern-matching, and to surface the 'same-plane' and direction misconceptions.
keyRepresentations: Coordinate/squared grid showing object and image together
Mirror line with perpendicular 'joining lines' to corresponding vertices (reflection)
Centre-of-rotation marked, with an angle arc and a direction arrow (rotation)
Translation vector arrow (displacement) applied to every vertex
Tracing paper as the physical model for rotation and for congruence checks
commonMisconceptions: Calling a rotation a reflection (or vice versa) because sense/handedness is not checked.
Describing a rotation incompletely — giving the angle but omitting the centre and/or the direction.
When reflecting in a sloping mirror, keeping the image in the same horizontal/vertical plane instead of moving each point perpendicular to the mirror.
Reversing coordinates (up before across) when labelling where the image landed.

learn.summary: Learners read a picture of a shape and its image on a squared/coordinate grid and say precisely WHICH transformation maps one onto the other, then work the other way — producing the image from a stated transformation. The defining evidence differs per transformation: reflection reverses 'sense' (handedness) and is built with a mirror line that is the perpendicular bisector of segments joining object and image points; translation keeps orientation and sense and is described by a vector/displacement applied to every vertex; rotation keeps sense but changes orientation and must be described by three things — centre, size (angle) of turn, and direction (clockwise/anticlockwise). Fluency means translating freely between the drawn image and its precise verbal description while checking congruence throughout, including non-standard cases such as sloping mirror lines and ambiguous turn directions.

activities.title: Name it: reconstruct the transformation that produced the image
feedback: If you named a reflection: ask 'does the shape read the same way round, or the mirror way round?' Only reflection reverses sense — re-decide from that check.

If you gave only the angle: a rotation needs three things — centre, size, direction. Add each and test by reproducing the image (tracing paper pinned at the centre lets you turn to the stated angle and direction and verify congruence).
If the image lands in the wrong place: check whether the centre is correct; if it turns the wrong way, check the direction.
Mark a rotation description as incomplete until centre, angle AND direction are all present.
activities.rationale: Identifying and describing a transformation is strengthened by setting the very parameters that define it and watching the image obey — binding each verbal descriptor to its visible effect. Mixing a reflection among rotations deliberately draws attention to what a rotation is not.
sourceClaims: A rotation must be described by three pieces of information — a centre of rotation, a size of turn, and a direction — and direction ambiguity (clockwise vs anticlockwise) is a documented difficulty.

Reflection is the only transformation that changes 'sense'; rotation changes orientation but maintains sense, and translation maintains congruence and orientation — so sense distinguishes rotation from reflection. Examples deliberately mix a reflection among rotations to draw attention to what a rotation is not.
learnerActions: On a grid showing a shape and its image already placed (produced by a rotation), work out which single transformation maps the first onto the second and reproduce it by setting the parameters yourself.
First try a reflection: flip the shape and compare handedness to the target — notice the 'sense' no longer matches (the target reads the same way round), so it cannot be a reflection.
Switch to rotation: choose a centre of rotation, set the angle of turn, and choose the direction (clockwise/anticlockwise) until your image lands exactly on the target.

State the full description aloud or in writing, e.g. 'rotation, 90° clockwise, about (2,1)', and check what each part controls: turning the same amount about a different centre makes the shape land somewhere else, and for a 90° turn, going the opposite direction lands it in a different place. (For a 180° turn, clockwise and anticlockwise give the same image, but still state the direction to keep the description complete.)
Confirm the image is congruent to the original (e.g. by tracing or matching vertices).
activities.intendedInsight: Checking sense is what distinguishes a rotation from a reflection, and a rotation is only fully specified by centre, size AND direction together. The centre and the angle always affect where the image lands. The direction matters for 90° turns, but a 180° turn lands in the same place either way.

activities.title: Produce a reflection in a sloping mirror line
feedback: If the image sits level with the object rather than square across a sloping mirror: your joining lines are not perpendicular to the mirror. Draw the perpendicular from each vertex and step the equal distance beyond.
Avoid 'straight across' language so the idea survives sloping mirror lines.
If sense is not reversed, you have not reflected — check the handedness of the image against the original.
activities.rationale: A frequent error is keeping the image in the same horizontal/vertical plane instead of moving each point perpendicular to the mirror; building the perpendicular-equidistant structure explicitly and testing it on a sloping line generalises the method.
sourceClaims: A common reflection misconception is keeping the image in the same vertical/horizontal plane rather than moving each point perpendicular to the mirror line; the mirror line is the perpendicular bisector of segments joining object and image points.
learnerActions: Given a shape and a mirror line (including sloping or offset lines, not just horizontal/vertical), draw the reflected image.
For each vertex, draw the perpendicular from the vertex to the mirror line and step an equal distance beyond it to place the image vertex.
Check that the mirror line is the perpendicular bisector of each segment joining a vertex to its image, and that the sense (handedness) of the shape is reversed.
Describe what you did as 'a reflection in [this] mirror line' and confirm the image is congruent to the original.
Repeat with a sloping mirror to make sure your method does not rely on 'straight across/down'.
activities.intendedInsight: A reflection moves every point perpendicular to the mirror by an equal distance on the other side, so the mirror is the perpendicular bisector of each joining segment — this holds for sloping mirrors, not just level ones.

activities.title: Translate by a vector and label coordinates carefully
feedback: If a landed vertex is reported as (up, across): re-anchor with 'across the corridor, then up the stairs' and re-check one labelled vertex together.
If only some vertices moved the right amount, remember the same displacement applies to every vertex.
activities.rationale: Reversing the ordered pair is a recurring coordinate error; anchoring 'across then up' and checking a vertex guards against it while reinforcing that translation preserves orientation and congruence.
sourceClaims: Reversing the ordered pair (reading the second coordinate before the first) is a recurring coordinate error to guard against.

Reflection is the only transformation that changes 'sense'; rotation changes orientation but maintains sense, and translation maintains congruence and orientation — so sense distinguishes rotation from reflection. Examples deliberately mix a reflection among rotations to draw attention to what a rotation is not.
learnerActions: Translate a shape by a given displacement (e.g. 3 right and 2 up), applying the same movement to every vertex.
Describe the movement both as a vector and in left/right/up/down words.
Label the coordinates of the translated vertices, writing each as (across, up).
Check that orientation and sense are unchanged and that the image is congruent to the original.
activities.intendedInsight: A translation slides every point by the same displacement, preserving orientation, sense and size; coordinates are read across first, then up.

activities.title: Precision check: discrete items for describing transformations
feedback: Score a rotation description as correct only if centre, angle AND direction are all present.
For the rotation-vs-reflection item, point to sense: if handedness flipped it is a reflection, if sense is unchanged it is a rotation.
activities.rationale: Discrete items are useful for checking precision of description and for surfacing the rotation-vs-reflection confusion via a sense-reversed distractor; on their own they check recognition and stated description rather than independent construction of the image.
sourceClaims: A rotation must be described by three pieces of information — a centre of rotation, a size of turn, and a direction — and direction ambiguity (clockwise vs anticlockwise) is a documented difficulty.
learnerActions: Answer 'which transformation maps A to B?' where one distractor shows the same shape reflected (sense reversed) rather than rotated.
Match written descriptions to images.
Fill in the three parts of a rotation description (centre, size, direction) for a shown image.
Draw the path/image to produce a reflection in a given mirror line.
activities.intendedInsight: Describing a transformation precisely means using the correct defining marks — and a rotation description counts only when centre, angle and direction are all given.

activities.title: Annotated worked examples as a reference
feedback: Answer 'rotation or reflection?' by checking whether sense reversed, then confirm against the revealed marks.
Treat this as a reference: to build the skill, move on to naming an unlabelled image and producing images yourself.
activities.rationale: A fixed annotated example cannot be manipulated by the learner, but it can make the defining marks and the sense check explicit and serve as a reference alongside generative tasks.
sourceClaims: Reflection is the only transformation that changes 'sense'; rotation changes orientation but maintains sense, and translation maintains congruence and orientation — so sense distinguishes rotation from reflection. Examples deliberately mix a reflection among rotations to draw attention to what a rotation is not.
learnerActions: Study one worked example of each transformation with its defining marks revealed: the mirror line and perpendicular joining lines for reflection; the vector arrow for translation; the centre, angle arc and direction arrow for rotation.
For each, identify whether the sense is reversed and use that to decide 'rotation or reflection?'.
Use these as a reference while attempting your own naming and producing tasks.
activities.intendedInsight: Each transformation has a distinct set of marks to read; sense reversal is the tell for reflection.

constraints: A complete rotation description requires all three parts — centre, size of turn, and direction; treat any missing part as incomplete.
Avoid 'straight across/down' language for reflection so methods generalise to sloping and offset mirror lines; use perpendicular-and-equidistant instead.
Label image coordinates consistently as (across, up) to guard against reversing the ordered pair.
Include non-standard cases (a turn that could be read clockwise or anticlockwise; a reflection in a sloping line) to force analysis rather than pattern-matching.
Discrete/recognition items (multiple choice, matching) check precision of stated description but do not by themselves elicit independent construction of an image; pair them with producing tasks.
Tracing paper (pin the centre, turn to the stated angle and direction) is a useful physical model for rotation and for checking congruence; it is a supportive tool, not a required mechanism.

Interactive controls (mode buttons, draggable mirror line, pinnable centre with angle dial and CW/ACW toggle, live sense indicator and congruence overlay) are optional ways to make the descriptor-to-motion link concrete; the same learning can be done on paper.

These transformations are planar and are read from marks on a grid, so a third dimension is not needed to read a mirror line, vector or centre. A dialogue/persona format can discuss and prompt transformation work but does not itself present or manipulate the grid, so producing an image would still happen on the learner's own paper. These are scoping affordance notes, not claims that any medium is uniquely necessary, superior, or impossible.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Source claims about sense/handedness, the three parts of a rotation, perpendicular-bisector reflection, and coordinate reversal are cited from NCETM materials as recorded in the source row; comparative efficacy of any specific activity format is not established by these citations.

Legacy 'fit' rankings asserting that a third dimension 'adds nothing' and that a conversation 'cannot' teach this were softened to scoped affordance notes; the source ratings do not establish universal necessity or impossibility.

The diagnostic and these activities assume a scalene/asymmetric shape so that sense and orientation changes are visible; ensure any chosen shape is asymmetric enough that reflection vs rotation genuinely differs, otherwise the sense check is not discriminating.
Note for 180° rotations specifically, clockwise and anticlockwise give the same image, so the 'direction turns it the wrong way' feedback applies to turns such as 90°, not to 180°.

probeDeeper: 'How can you be sure this is a rotation and not a reflection?' (listen for sense/handedness as the deciding evidence, not orientation alone).
'If I only told you the shape was rotated 90°, could you draw exactly where it lands? What else do you need?' (elicits centre and direction as required parameters).

Counterexample: 'Your friend says the second shape is a reflection. Show me the mirror line that would do it — does one exist?' (a rotated shape has no consistent mirror line; the search exposes the error).
'Is the image congruent to the original after your reflection? How would you check?' (tracing/matching; congruence is invariant under all three transformations).
assess.correctAnswer: For the shown image: 'a rotation' named with all three descriptors — centre (the marked point), size (90°/quarter turn) and direction (clockwise or anticlockwise, matching the picture) — justified by the shape keeping its sense while changing orientation. For the produced reflection: each vertex placed perpendicular to and equidistant from the mirror, sense reversed, described as a reflection in that mirror line, and the image confirmed congruent to the original.

responseLevels.gap: Cannot reliably name the transformation — confuses rotation and reflection, or offers only a bare word with no defining marks — and cannot produce a correct reflection (image not perpendicular/equidistant, sense not reversed).
responseLevels.full: Names each transformation from its evidence (using sense to separate rotation from reflection), describes a rotation completely (centre, size, direction), produces a reflection with each vertex perpendicular and equidistant and sense reversed, labels image coordinates as (across, up), and confirms congruence — transferring correctly to non-standard mirror lines and centres.
responseLevels.partial: Reads and names each transformation and can produce a reflection in a vertical/horizontal mirror, but treats the descriptors as a checklist rather than a structure — e.g. identifies a rotation yet omits centre or direction, or produces a reflection correctly only in standard positions while failing a sloping mirror. Lists the parts of a transformation but cannot yet explain how they jointly fix the image or transfer to a non-standard case.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Show a squared grid with a scalene shape and its image, where the image is the shape turned a quarter-turn about a marked point (sense unchanged). Say: 'What single transformation maps the first shape onto the second? Describe it as fully as you can.' Then give a fresh copy of the original next to a mirror line and say: 'Now YOU produce the reflection of this shape in this mirror line, and describe what you did.' Read what they say about the shown transformation, then watch what they draw.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The reading move forces a choice between rotation and reflection that only checking SENSE resolves — a child who reasons from sense names it correctly, one who guesses from orientation alone may call it a reflection. Requiring a FULL description exposes whether the child knows a rotation needs centre, angle and direction, not just the word. The producing move then shows whether they can generate the perpendicular-equidistant structure themselves, so reading and producing are checked separately.

Identify which of a pinwheel, a heart and an equilateral triangle have rotational symmetry

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Transformations on a Grid
topic.description: Identify, describe, and represent the position of a shape following a reflection or translation using appropriate language; know that the shape has not changed
evidence: Reflect a triangle in a vertical mirror line on a coordinate grid and state the new coordinates
Translate a shape 3 units right and 2 units up and describe the movement
Explain that a reflected/translated shape is congruent to the original
topic.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} slides or flips a shape on squared paper, can they describe exactly where it ends up and confirm the shape itself hasn't changed size or angles?

pedagogy.summary: Children reflect and translate a shape on a squared grid, give the image's coordinates, and articulate that the moved shape is congruent to the original — same size and shape, only its position (and, for reflection, its sense) has changed. The pedagogical heart is that a transformation is a rule for where every point goes, not a vague 'slide it over': reflection sends each vertex perpendicularly across the mirror line to an equal distance on the far side, and translation sends every vertex the same distance in the same direction. Congruence is the invariant that makes both trustworthy.
bestPractices: Build reflection from the point rule, not 'flip it': for each vertex, draw the line to the mirror, note it is PERPENDICULAR to the mirror, count the squares to the line, then count the same number of squares beyond it — the image vertex lands there. Assemble the image vertex by vertex.

Explicitly avoid the language 'straight across' or 'straight down' even for vertical/horizontal mirrors; say 'perpendicular to the mirror line' so the idea generalises when mirror lines later slope (NCETM KS3 6.3).

Draw attention to 'sense': after a reflection the shape reads the mirror-image way round (a clockwise vertex order becomes anticlockwise). This is what distinguishes a true reflection from a shape that has merely been slid across.

Establish translation as 'every point moves the same' — model it by moving ONE vertex '5 right, 2 up', then checking every other vertex followed the identical move; the shape's orientation and sense are unchanged.
Make congruence explicit and testable: trace the original onto tracing paper and lay it over the image to confirm same size and shape; name the word 'congruent'.
Keep coordinate reading disciplined — state the image coordinates as (across, up), guarding against the x-y reversal that surfaces whenever coordinates re-enter.
keyRepresentations: Squared/coordinate grid with a vertical (then horizontal) mirror line
Perpendicular 'joining lines' from each object vertex to its image vertex, crossed at right angles by the mirror line
Tracing paper laid over object and image to demonstrate congruence
A translation vector shown as a 'staircase' arrow (e.g. 5 right then 2 up) applied identically to every vertex
commonMisconceptions: Reflecting by sliding the shape across the mirror unchanged, so its sense is not reversed (translate-instead-of-flip).
Placing the image the wrong distance from the mirror — not equidistant — often by miscounting or letting the shape touch the line.
Believing the shape changes size or becomes a 'different shape' once moved, rather than staying congruent.
Reversing the image coordinates (writing y before x) when reporting where the shape landed.

learn.summary: Year 5 learners reflect and translate a scalene shape on a squared/coordinate grid, state the image coordinates as (across, up), and justify that the moved shape is congruent — same size and shape, with only its position (and, for reflection, its sense) changed. The core idea is that a transformation is a precise rule for where every point goes: reflection sends each vertex perpendicularly across the mirror line to an equal distance on the far side, and translation sends every vertex the same distance in the same direction. Congruence is the invariant that makes both trustworthy.

activities.title: Build a reflection vertex by vertex using the perpendicular-equidistant rule
feedback: If the image reads the same way round as the original (sense not reversed), it is not a reflection. It was most likely slid (or possibly turned) rather than reflected. Rebuild it one vertex at a time using the perpendicular lines so the reversal emerges from the rule. Avoid 'straight across/down' language; say 'perpendicular to the mirror line'.
If the square-counts from the mirror differ between an object vertex and its image, or the image touches the mirror line, recount perpendicular to the line on each side and make the two counts equal.

If coordinates come out as (up, across) — e.g. a corner at (5,3) reported as '(3,5)' while the plotted point is correct — re-anchor 'across first, then up' and recheck one corner together against the grid.
activities.rationale: Teaching reflection from the perpendicular point-rule, and explicitly avoiding 'straight across/down' language, targets the documented misconception that the image stays in the same vertical/horizontal plane and generalises to sloping mirror lines later. Using a scalene shape makes the reversal of sense observable; of the two transformations in this unit, only reflection reverses sense.
sourceClaims: A common reflection misconception is that the image stays in the same vertical/horizontal plane rather than moving perpendicular to the mirror; the remedy is to teach that every line joining a point to its image is perpendicular to the mirror line and to avoid 'straight across/down' language.

Reflection uniquely reverses 'sense' — a feature able to change only under reflection — whereas translation maintains congruence and orientation; this distinguishes a genuine reflection from a shape merely slid across.
The mirror line is the perpendicular bisector of the segments joining object and image vertices (lines joining equivalent points are parallel and the mirror is perpendicular to them).
A recurring coordinate error is reversing the ordered pair (writing/reading the second value before the first); teaching should reinforce reading across before up.
learnerActions: Start with a scalene triangle on a squared grid and a vertical mirror line two squares to its right (choose scalene so a reversal of sense is visible).

For each vertex in turn, draw the line from the vertex to the mirror line that meets the mirror at a right angle (perpendicular to the mirror line); with this vertical mirror it runs along a horizontal grid line. Check the right angle rather than assuming it.
Count the squares from the vertex to the mirror along that perpendicular, then count the SAME number of squares beyond the mirror and mark the image vertex there.
Repeat for every vertex, then join the image vertices to complete the reflected shape.

Compare the vertex order: check that the image reads the mirror-image way round (a clockwise order of corners becomes anticlockwise) — this reversed 'sense' is what makes it a true reflection rather than a slide.
State the coordinates of each image corner as (across, up), reading across first then up.
activities.intendedInsight: A reflection is produced point by point: every line joining an object vertex to its image is perpendicular to the mirror line, and the image vertex is the same distance beyond the mirror as the object is in front. Because this reverses the vertex order, the shape's sense flips — distinguishing a genuine reflection from a shape merely slid across.

activities.title: Translate every point by the same vector and contrast it with reflection
feedback: If only part of the shape moves, or vertices move by different amounts, re-apply the single vector to each vertex in turn until every corner has shifted identically.
If a learner claims the translated shape has 'turned', check the vertex order against the original: a translation leaves it reading the same way round.
Prompt: 'Is your translated triangle congruent to the reflected one as well as to the original? How do you know?' — both transformations preserve size and shape.
activities.rationale: Modelling translation as 'every point moves the same' and directly contrasting it with reflection isolates the invariant (orientation/sense preserved) that separates the two transformations. The curriculum expects Year 5 pupils to translate shapes and recognise the result is congruent.
sourceClaims: Reflection uniquely reverses 'sense' — a feature able to change only under reflection — whereas translation maintains congruence and orientation; this distinguishes a genuine reflection from a shape merely slid across.
Year 5 pupils should reflect and translate shapes and recognise that the translated/reflected shape is congruent (unchanged in size and shape).
learnerActions: Take the original triangle and set a single translation rule, e.g. '5 squares right, 2 squares up', shown as a staircase arrow.
Apply that identical move to ONE vertex first, then check that every other vertex has to follow the exact same move.
Complete the translated shape and confirm its orientation and sense are unchanged (it reads the same way round as the original).
Place the reflected shape and the translated shape side by side and describe the felt difference: the slide keeps sense, the flip reverses it.
Report the translated image coordinates as (across, up).
activities.intendedInsight: A translation moves every point the same distance in the same direction, so orientation and sense are unchanged — the opposite of reflection, which reverses sense. Both leave the shape congruent to the original.

activities.title: Test congruence by tracing and overlaying
feedback: If a learner says the moved shape is bigger, smaller, or 'different', lay the tracing directly over the image (turning it over for a reflection) to show the exact match, then name 'congruent'.
For a reflected image the tracing must be flipped over to match — note that this flip IS the reversed sense, and the shape is still congruent.
If a learner can overlay correctly but resists the word, restate: position changed, size and shape did not — that is what congruent means.
activities.rationale: A direct physical match makes congruence testable rather than asserted, targeting the misconception that moving a shape changes it. Tracing paper or a card cutout is a concrete approximation of the ideal flat figure, which has zero thickness; the demonstration is about the mathematical shape represented, not the physical copy.
sourceClaims: Year 5 pupils should reflect and translate shapes and recognise that the translated/reflected shape is congruent (unchanged in size and shape).
learnerActions: Trace the original triangle onto tracing paper (or cut out a card copy, noting that real paper/card has slight thickness and only approximates the ideal zero-thickness flat figure it represents).

Lay the tracing directly over the translated image and confirm an exact match in size and shape; for the reflected image, turn the tracing paper OVER to make it match — this flip is itself the reversed sense, and the size and shape are still identical.
Say aloud that the moved shape is congruent to the original: only its position (and, for the reflection, its sense) has changed, not its size or shape.
Answer the challenge 'Is it a new, different triangle now?' — about the mathematical shape represented — by pointing to the exact overlay match.
activities.intendedInsight: Reflection and translation change where a shape is (and reflection changes which way round it reads) but never its size or shape; the technical word for this sameness is 'congruent'.

activities.title: Diagnostic performance task: reflect, translate, and justify
feedback: Watch how the image is built rather than explaining the rule first; a block-shunted image reading the same way round signals a slide-instead-of-reflect error to reteach via the perpendicular rule.

Full response: each reflected vertex perpendicular and equidistant with sense reversed, every translated vertex moved identically, coordinates as (across, up), congruence justified by matching/tracing, and correct transfer when the mirror line or vector changes.

Partial response: carries out both transformations and may name congruence but treats each as a remembered procedure — cannot say WHY the image sits where it does or transfer to a mirror in a new position; reteach the point rule explicitly.
If coordinates are reversed, re-anchor 'across first, then up' and check one vertex together.
activities.rationale: A watch-the-build performance task discriminates genuine understanding of the point rule from imitation, because the two documented misconceptions (unreversed sense; unequal distance from the mirror) show up in how the image is constructed. Probing the perpendicular relationship and congruence surfaces reasoning rather than recall.

learnerActions: Given a squared grid showing a scalene triangle and a vertical mirror line two squares to its right, reflect the triangle in the mirror line and state the coordinates of the reflected corners as (across, up).
Back with the original, translate it 5 squares right and 2 squares up, and describe the move made.
Explain whether the new triangle is the same as the first and how you know, using tracing/overlay and the word congruent.

Answer probes: What is the relationship between the line joining a corner to its image and the mirror line? If the mirror moved one square further right, what would happen to the reflected triangle? If a friend slid the triangle across without turning it, is that a reflection, and how can you tell?
activities.intendedInsight: Holding the perpendicular-equidistant rule produces an image that is both the correct distance AND reversed in sense; merely sliding produces the wrong sense (and often the wrong distance). Watching HOW the image is assembled — perpendicular vertex by vertex, or shunted as a whole block — separates understanding from imitation, and the congruence question separates learners who see the shape as invariant from those who think moving changes it.

constraints: Use a scalene shape so the reversal of sense is visible; a symmetric shape can hide whether a learner reflected or merely slid.
Say 'perpendicular to the mirror line' rather than 'straight across/down', even for vertical or horizontal mirrors, so the rule generalises to sloping mirror lines later.
Report image coordinates as (across, up), guarding against the x-before-y / y-before-x reversal.
When using tracing paper to check a reflection, the tracing must be turned OVER to overlay the image; the shape remains congruent and that flip is the reversed sense.

Discrete-item checks (choosing the correctly reflected image among a slid-across distractor and a not-equidistant distractor, filling in image coordinates, true/false on congruence) can diagnose the two misconceptions but, because nothing recomputes, they check rather than build the felt rule; use them alongside, not instead of, construction.

A pre-annotated worked diagram that reveals the perpendicular joining lines, the equal square-counts and the label 'congruent' can illustrate the rule but does not let a learner test their own placement, which is the core skill; treat it as a scaffold, not the assessment.

A live grid where dragging a vertex or the mirror line recomputes the image (with faint perpendicular joining lines, live square-counts that turn green when the two sides match, a sense badge that flips when the reflection is correct, a settable translation arrow applied to all vertices at once, and a ghost of the original for congruence) can make the invariants concrete; these interaction and feedback examples are optional ways to expose the mechanism, not mandatory.

Tracing paper or a card cutout is a concrete approximation of the ideal flat (zero-thickness) figure; use it to demonstrate congruence of the represented mathematical shape while distinguishing that shape from the physical copy.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

One legacy source claim (National Curriculum, Year 5 reflect/translate/congruence) was marked verified:false in the row and is cited in Activities 2, 3 and 4; it directly supports the congruence principle and is the only curriculum source for it, but its evidential status is unconfirmed, so treat its citation accordingly.

The legacy entry framed a 3D rendering and an in-role dialogue as 'poor' for this planar skill. Those are catalog-fit judgements, not universal laws: a planar grid is well suited to square-counting and depth is not used here, but no claim of universal impossibility is made. These alternatives were not carried forward as activities because they do not let the learner construct and verify a reflection; their underlying affordances are noted only as scaffolds/limits.

Legacy phrasing such as 'cannot let the child TEST their own placement' and 'adds nothing' was softened to scoped affordance/limit statements; the exact sources do not establish comparative efficacy or necessity.

The row's evidence statement gives a '3 units right, 2 units up' translation example, whereas the diagnostic and these activities use '5 right, 2 up'; the activities follow the diagnostic consistently.

probeDeeper: Point at one object vertex and its image and ask: 'What can you tell me about the line joining these two corners and the mirror line?' (listen for perpendicular / equal distance, not 'it's across from it').
'If I moved the mirror line one square further right, what would happen to your reflected triangle?' (tests that the image is defined by distance from the mirror, not a fixed spot).
Counterexample: 'Your friend slid the triangle straight across to here without turning it round — is that a reflection? How can you tell?' (listen for sense/orientation reversal being absent).
'You translated it 5 right and 2 up. Is the translated triangle congruent to the reflected one as well as to the original? How do you know?' (congruence is preserved by both transformations).
assess.correctAnswer: The child places each reflected vertex perpendicularly opposite its original at an equal number of squares beyond the mirror line, so the image is equidistant and its sense is reversed (a scalene triangle visibly reads the other way round); reports the image coordinates as (across, up); translates by moving every vertex 5 right and 2 up together; and states the moved shape is congruent — same size and shape — checking by matching or tracing, understanding only position (and, for the reflection, orientation/sense) changed.

errorPatterns.nextMove: Draw the line from one vertex to the mirror, show it meets the mirror at a right angle, count the squares and count the same beyond; repeat per vertex so the reversed sense emerges from the rule. Avoid 'straight across' language.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The image reads the SAME way round as the original (vertex order not reversed) — for a scalene triangle the 'point' faces the same direction; the child moves the shape as one block rather than vertex by vertex.

errorPatterns.pattern: Places the image the wrong distance from the mirror — not equidistant — often letting the shape touch the line or miscounting one side
errorPatterns.nextMove: Count squares perpendicular from each vertex to the line, then step the identical count to the far side; mark both counts and compare.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Square-counts from mirror differ between object and image; image sits closer to or on the mirror line.

errorPatterns.nextMove: Trace the original and lay it over the image to show an exact match; name 'congruent' — position (and sense) changed, size and shape did not.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says the moved shape is bigger/smaller or 'different'; cannot justify sameness or resists the word congruent.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reverses the reported image coordinates, giving the up-value before the across-value

errorPatterns.revealedBy: States a landed vertex as (up, across) — e.g. calls (5,3) '(3,5)' — while the plotted point is actually correct.

responseLevels.gap: Cannot place a correct image: slides the shape across with unchanged sense or at an unequal distance, and treats the moved shape as changed or 'new'. Coordinates may also be reversed.
