pedagogy.summary: Children operate transformations as rules on coordinates: translating a shape changes every vertex by adding/subtracting the horizontal and vertical moves (right +x, left −x, up +y, down −y), while reflecting in an axis changes the sign of exactly ONE coordinate — reflection in the x-axis sends (x, y) to (x, −y), reflection in the y-axis sends (x, y) to (−x, y). The conceptual anchor is that the axis you reflect IN is the mirror, points move PERPENDICULAR to it, and so the coordinate measuring distance from that mirror flips sign while the other is unchanged. Fluency means predicting image coordinates from the rule and explaining why each rule takes the form it does.
bestPractices: Derive the sign rules from the geometry, not memorised swaps: reflecting in the x-axis flips the shape VERTICALLY, so the vertical (y) coordinate changes sign and x stays; reflecting in the y-axis flips it HORIZONTALLY, so x changes sign and y stays.
Tie the rule to equal distance: the image is the same distance from the axis as the original, on the opposite side — (x, y) and (x, −y) are both |y| from the x-axis (Oak National Academy).

Explicitly separate the two axis rules with worked pairs — e.g. (−4, 1) reflects to (4, 1) in the y-axis but to (−4, −1) in the x-axis — so pupils feel which single coordinate changes each time (Oak).

Confront reflection-as-translation head-on with examples and non-examples: a slid shape keeps its orientation, a reflected shape is reversed; use real mirrors as a scaffold, then move to reasoning with coordinates (Oak).
For translation, treat each direction as a signed change to the matching coordinate — '2 down' subtracts 2 from y — and have pupils PREDICT image coordinates before plotting.
Avoid 'straight across/down' language; say points move perpendicular to the mirror line, so the correct coordinate change is understood rather than transposed (NCETM KS3 6.3).
keyRepresentations: Four-quadrant coordinate grid with the x- and y-axes as mirror lines

Real mirror / Mira placed on an axis to check the image, as a scaffold

commonMisconceptions: Reflecting in the x-axis but changing the sign of the WRONG coordinate (negating x instead of y), effectively reflecting in the other axis.
Reflecting by sliding/translating the shape rather than reflecting it, so the image is not reversed.
Getting the translation sign wrong — adding when the move is left or down instead of subtracting.
Reversing the coordinate pair (writing the y-value before the x-value) when stating image vertices.

learn.summary: Year 6 pupils learn to translate shapes on a four-quadrant coordinate grid (adding/subtracting signed amounts to matching coordinates) and to reflect shapes in the x- or y-axis by negating exactly one coordinate. The goal is to DERIVE the sign rules from geometry — points move perpendicular to the mirror axis, so the coordinate measuring distance from that axis flips sign while the other stays — rather than memorise a swap. Core errors: changing the wrong coordinate (reflecting in the wrong axis), sliding instead of reflecting (no reversal), wrong translation signs for left/down moves, and reversing the ordered pair.

activities.title: Predict, then reflect: watch the single coordinate flip
feedback: If a predicted point lands in the wrong quadrant, diagonally opposite the true image (e.g. (4, 1) in the first quadrant instead of (−4, −1) in the third for an x-axis reflection), you likely negated the wrong coordinate — ask which direction the shape actually moves and which coordinate measures distance from that axis.
If the image keeps facing the same way (not mirrored), you slid/translated instead of reflecting; rebuild one vertex at an equal perpendicular distance on the opposite side so the reversal appears.
Check the image and original are the same distance from the axis and the same size and shape — e.g. (x, y) and (x, −y) are both |y| from the x-axis.
activities.rationale: Acting on a shape and watching the coordinate table update makes the single-coordinate sign change visible, and predicting first surfaces the wrong-coordinate and slide-not-reflect misconceptions as a visibly misplaced point. Contrasting the SAME vertex reflected in each axis separates the two rules by reasoning rather than memorised swap. A live table, ghost original, and predict-mode are optional supports that make the mechanism concrete.
sourceClaims: The most common mistake pupils make when reflecting is to flip/translate the shape rather than reflect it; the reflection and original should be the same distance from the axis and the same size and shape, and real mirrors help pupils notice the direction the reflection faces.

Reflecting a vertex at (−4,1) in the y-axis gives (4,1) (only x changes sign) while reflecting it in the x-axis gives (−4,−1) (only y changes sign); reflecting in both axes gives (4,−1). Distractor answers that change the wrong coordinate correspond to the classic 'wrong coordinate / wrong axis' error.

Reflection should be taught via the perpendicular structure — every line joining a point to its image is perpendicular to the mirror line — avoiding 'straight across/down' language, so the correct coordinate change is derived rather than memorised; examples should span all quadrants and the axes.
learnerActions: On a four-quadrant grid, start with a triangle plotted in the second quadrant and its vertices labelled with coordinates.
Before anything moves, choose 'reflect in the x-axis' and write down what you predict each vertex will become.
Run the reflection: watch each vertex move perpendicular to the x-axis (vertically, to the opposite side) while, in a coordinate table, only the y-value changes sign and x stays the same.
If a real mirror or Mira is available, stand it on the x-axis to check the image faces the opposite way and sits the same distance from the axis.
Now, starting from the SAME triangle, reflect in the y-axis instead and predict again: this time the shape flips sideways (perpendicular to the y-axis) and only x changes sign.
Compare the two results on the same vertex, e.g. (−4, 1) → (−4, −1) in the x-axis but (−4, 1) → (4, 1) in the y-axis.
activities.intendedInsight: Reflecting in the x-axis flips the shape vertically, so the y-coordinate (vertical distance from the x-axis) negates and x is unchanged; reflecting in the y-axis flips it horizontally, so x negates and y is unchanged. The axis you reflect IN is the mirror and points move perpendicular to it.

activities.title: Translate by signed changes — predict before plotting
feedback: If a '2 down' move made the y-value increase, you added instead of subtracted — down and left reduce the coordinate; re-predict then check one vertex on the grid.
If the whole shape moved but didn't reverse, that is correct for a translation — a translation never produces a mirror image.
Check each vertex against the grid before trusting the rule.
activities.rationale: Predicting signed coordinate changes before plotting targets the add-when-it-should-subtract error and distinguishes a slide (orientation preserved) from a reflection (orientation reversed).
learnerActions: Take a triangle on the grid and a translation instruction such as '3 squares right and 2 squares down'.
Treat each direction as a signed change to the matching coordinate: right adds to x, left subtracts from x, up adds to y, down subtracts from y. So '3 right, 2 down' gives (x, y) → (x+3, y−2).
Predict the new coordinates of every vertex BEFORE plotting, then plot and check against the grid.
Say back how the whole shape kept its orientation (a slide does not reverse the shape).
activities.intendedInsight: Translation adds or subtracts a signed amount to the matching coordinate and preserves orientation; left and down are negative changes, not additions.

activities.title: Contrast slide versus reflect, and keep the pair in order
feedback: If you reported a vertex as (y, x) though the plotted point looks right, re-anchor 'x before y, along then up/down' and recheck.
If an on-axis point moved, remember a point on the mirror is already on it, so its distance from the axis is zero and it does not move.
Use examples and non-examples (and a real mirror on the axis) to confirm the reflection faces the other way.
activities.rationale: Pairing reflection against translation on the same shape elicits the reversal/equidistance idea versus a straight slide, and explicit (x, y) ordering guards against the common pair-reversal interference error. The on-axis fixed-point case is a useful boundary check.
sourceClaims: The most common mistake pupils make when reflecting is to flip/translate the shape rather than reflect it; the reflection and original should be the same distance from the axis and the same size and shape, and real mirrors help pupils notice the direction the reflection faces.
A recurring coordinate error is reversing the ordered pair (stating the second value before the first); guard against it with 'x before y / along then up'.
learnerActions: Reflect a triangle in the x-axis and separately translate the same triangle 'down' by a fixed amount; place the two results side by side.
Describe how they differ: the reflected image is reversed and equidistant on the opposite side of the axis; the translated image faces the same way and simply slid.
Find a vertex that sits ON the mirror axis, e.g. (0, 4) on the y-axis, and reflect in that axis: note it stays fixed.
When listing every image vertex, write x before y ('along then up/down') and check one plotted point matches the pair you wrote.
activities.intendedInsight: Reflection reverses sense and is equidistant across the mirror; translation preserves sense. Points on the mirror axis map to themselves. Ordered pairs are always (x, y).

activities.title: Diagnose with paired axis items (assessment)
feedback: Choosing (4, 1) for an x-axis reflection means you changed x instead of y — you effectively reflected in the y-axis; re-anchor to the vertical flip.
Choosing (−1, −4) means you swapped the coordinate order of the correct image (−4, −1); apply 'x before y'.
A correct choice or plot with no 'why' is not yet secure — ask for the perpendicular/equidistance reason.
activities.rationale: Multiple-choice items whose distractors ARE the misconceptions diagnose cleanly, and the draw-and-list step adds some image construction. However, selecting among options does not by itself build the felt derivation of why one coordinate changes, so pair this assessment with the predict-and-construct activities above.
sourceClaims: Reflecting a vertex at (−4,1) in the y-axis gives (4,1) (only x changes sign) while reflecting it in the x-axis gives (−4,−1) (only y changes sign); reflecting in both axes gives (4,−1). Distractor answers that change the wrong coordinate correspond to the classic 'wrong coordinate / wrong axis' error.
learnerActions: Answer items such as '(−4, 1) reflected in the x-axis = ?' where the correct answer is (−4, −1), the wrong-coordinate answer (4, 1) and the reversed-pair answer (−1, −4) are offered as options.
Complete fill-in-the-blank image coordinates after a stated translation.
Plot a reflection by drawing the image, then list its vertices.
Explain in words why only one coordinate changed for each reflection.
activities.intendedInsight: Picking the correct image while rejecting wrong-axis and reversed-pair distractors, plotting the image correctly, and explaining why only one coordinate changes together show the rule is reasoned rather than guessed.

constraints: Reflection and translation here are 2-D coordinate operations on the plane; a third dimension (z-values, planes of reflection) is not needed and distracts from the (x, y) sign rules.

Avoid 'straight across / straight down' as a generic rule; say points move perpendicular to the mirror axis so the correct coordinate change is understood rather than transposed (for the x-axis this motion happens to be vertical, for the y-axis horizontal).

Recognition/multiple-choice items diagnose and check but do not themselves elicit independent construction of an image or an explanation; use them alongside tasks where the child predicts, plots and justifies.
A real mirror or Mira is a helpful scaffold for noticing reversal and equidistance, but pupils should progress to reasoning directly with coordinates.

A static annotated grid can label a vertex's image and its coordinate change on tap, but it cannot let the child predict and test their own image, which is where the sign confusion lives — treat it as a supporting illustration, not the main task.

Self-audit of worked coordinates: (−4, 1) reflected in x-axis → (−4, −1); reflected in y-axis → (4, 1); in both → (4, −1); these are internally consistent across pedagogy, assess and sources. '3 right, 2 down' maps (x, y) → (x+3, y−2) — consistent with the diagnostic.
Reversed-pair distractor: the order-swap of the correct image (−4, −1) is (−1, −4); an earlier draft listed (1, −4), which is not a reversed pair and was fixed in activity 4.

Activity 4 contains both recognition (multiple-choice) and production (draw-and-list) steps; its stated limitation is scoped to the multiple-choice selection only, not to the whole activity, to avoid implying the activity never elicits construction.
The 'reflect in the x-axis flips vertically so y changes' reasoning is sound geometrically; retained as derivation, not as an unverified claim of comparative teaching efficacy.

The UK National Curriculum source is verified:false in the row and only establishes the curriculum expectation that Year 6 pupils translate and reflect shapes; it does not support the teaching principle in activity 2, so activity 2's sourceClaims is [].

On-axis fixed-point case ((0,4) reflected in the y-axis stays fixed) was present only in the assessment probes; added as a boundary check in an activity because it is mathematically correct and pedagogically useful.

probeDeeper: 'You reflected in the x-axis and the y-coordinates changed sign. Why that coordinate and not the x?' (listen for vertical flip / perpendicular-to-the-axis reasoning, not a recited rule).
Counterexample: 'Now reflect the SAME triangle in the y-axis instead. What changes this time?' (tests that the child does not apply the x-axis rule to both).
'Reflecting in the x-axis moves the triangle downward, and translating 2 down also moves it downward. How are the two results different?' (elicits reversal/equidistance versus a straight slide).

assess.correctAnswer: For the translation, each vertex gains 3 on x and loses 2 on y (right +x, down −y). For the reflection in the x-axis, each vertex keeps its x and negates its y — (x, y) → (x, −y) — so the image sits the same distance below the axis as the original is above, reversed in sense. The child explains that translating adds/subtracts to the coordinates while reflecting in the x-axis changes the sign of the y-coordinate only (and reflecting in the y-axis would change x only), because points move perpendicular to the mirror axis.

pedagogy.summary: KS3 transformations pull translation, rotation and reflection into one family unified by the idea that all three are RIGID motions producing a CONGRUENT image (same lengths and angles), differing only in what they do to position, orientation and 'sense' (handedness). Best taught by making each transformation's defining data explicit — a translation needs a vector, a reflection needs a mirror line, a rotation needs a centre, an angle and a direction — and by using 'sense' (whether the shape is flipped) as the single test that separates a reflection from a rotation. Extend beyond the horizontal/vertical mirrors of KS2 to diagonal mirror lines (y=x, y=−x) so pupils stop treating reflection as 'the same shape moved straight across'.

learn.summary: KS3 pupils learn to identify, describe and perform the three rigid plane transformations — translation, reflection and rotation — treating them as one family that produces a CONGRUENT image (same lengths and angles) and differs only in effect on position, orientation and 'sense' (handedness). The core teaching moves: insist every transformation be fully specified by its defining data (translation = column vector; reflection = equation of mirror line; rotation = centre + angle + direction), use sense (whether the shape is flipped) as the test separating reflection from rotation, treat the mirror line as the perpendicular bisector of each point→image segment, and extend beyond horizontal/vertical mirrors to diagonal mirrors (y=x, y=−x) and off-shape rotation centres. A clearly-handed scalene shape (an 'F' or a flag) on a four-quadrant grid makes a flipped vs unflipped image visible at a glance.

activities.title: Reflect, then try to copy it with a rotation
feedback: If the reflected image is a slide or an axis-aligned flip rather than the true reflection in y=x (coordinates not swapped), reteach the mirror line as the perpendicular bisector of each point→image segment: fold tracing paper along y=x to check, and contrast y=x with y=−x so horizontal/vertical is not treated as the only case.

If the shape's handedness is reversed yet the pupil still calls it a rotation (or vice versa), use the tracing-paper test: trace the shape and turn the tracing — a rotation can be laid exactly on top, a reflection cannot without flipping the paper over.
If the pupil claims the rotation reproduces the reflection, point to the sense marker: the rotated 'F' is not mirror-imaged, so the shapes do not match.
activities.rationale: A handed shape makes a wrong sense visible at a glance, and directly juxtaposing a reflection with an attempted rotation of the same object targets the misconception that rotation and reflection are interchangeable 'moves to over there'. Building the perpendicular-bisector guides for each vertex generalises reflection beyond H/V mirrors.
sourceClaims: Sense reverses ONLY under reflection (the test separating rotation from reflection); a rotation needs three pieces — centre, size and direction; reflecting in a diagonal mirror must not leave the image 'in the same vertical or horizontal plane' (a named misconception from overuse of H/V mirrors); the mirror line is the perpendicular bisector of each point-to-image segment; rigid transformations preserve congruence
learnerActions: On a four-quadrant coordinate grid, take a scalene, obviously-handed shape (an 'F' or a flag) and reflect it in the line y=x, recording the image coordinates of each vertex (e.g. (1,4) maps to (4,1) — for y=x, swap the coordinates).

For each vertex not lying on the mirror line, draw the segment from the point to its image and check it meets the mirror line at a right angle, crossing at the midpoint — confirming the mirror is the perpendicular bisector of every such point→image segment (a vertex on y=x maps to itself, so it has no segment).
Note whether the shape's handedness has changed: for the reflection the 'F' should appear mirror-imaged.

Now try to land the ORIGINAL shape on top of your reflected image using a ROTATION instead: pin a centre, choose 90° clockwise, and compare. Observe that the rotated shape keeps its handedness and so cannot coincide with the flipped reflection.
State in your own words why reflection and rotation give different results here: one reverses sense (handedness), the other preserves it.
activities.intendedInsight: Reflection reverses sense while rotation and translation preserve it; this handedness test is what distinguishes a reflection from a rotation even when the image lands in a similar place. Reflecting in y=x swaps the x and y coordinates (reflection in y=−x swaps and negates them: (x,y)→(−y,−x)), not merely slides the shape across.

activities.title: Fully describe a rotation — centre, angle and direction
feedback: If the description omits the centre or the direction (e.g. 'I rotated it 90°'), require all three pieces every time; show two 90° rotations about different centres landing differently so the centre is felt as essential.
If the pupil assumes clockwise by default, prompt them to state the direction explicitly, since anticlockwise would give a different image.
If finding the centre is difficult, remind them that the centre lies on the perpendicular bisector of every point→image segment, so intersecting two such bisectors locates it.
activities.rationale: Turning 'describe the rotation' into a construction (intersecting perpendicular bisectors) and contrasting two different centres both make the defining data concrete rather than nominal, addressing the common under-specification of rotations.
sourceClaims: Sense reverses ONLY under reflection (the test separating rotation from reflection); a rotation needs three pieces — centre, size and direction; reflecting in a diagonal mirror must not leave the image 'in the same vertical or horizontal plane' (a named misconception from overuse of H/V mirrors); the mirror line is the perpendicular bisector of each point-to-image segment; rigid transformations preserve congruence
learnerActions: Rotate the original shape 90° clockwise about the point (0,0) and describe exactly what you did, naming the centre, the angle AND the direction (clockwise/anticlockwise).
Check that your description is complete enough for someone else to reproduce the image uniquely: 'a rotation of 90° clockwise about the origin'.
Carry out two 90° rotations of the same shape about two different centres and compare where the image lands, to feel why the centre is essential and not optional.
Given only an object and its image, reconstruct the centre of rotation by joining two or more object points to their images and intersecting the perpendicular bisectors of those segments.
activities.intendedInsight: A rotation is not fully described — and cannot be uniquely reproduced — without its centre, angle and direction (direction can only be left out for a 180° turn, where both directions give the same image). The centre genuinely changes where the image lands, and can be found by construction.

activities.title: Translate and prove congruence
feedback: If image coordinates come out as the correct point with the pair reversed (e.g. recording (4,1) as (1,4)), separate this coordinate-recording slip from the transformation itself (which may be correct) and reteach x before y when recording every coordinate.

If the pupil asserts congruence without evidence, press: 'Are the object and image exactly the same size and shape? How could you PROVE it, not just look?' — expecting a tracing-paper overlay or a measurement of corresponding sides and angles.
If the pupil thinks a rigid transformation can change the shape's size, revisit that translation, reflection and rotation leave all lengths and angles unchanged by definition.
activities.rationale: Explicitly checking lengths and angles after a transformation names the image congruent to the object and counters the misconception that a rigid motion can resize a shape; keeping coordinate reversal separate avoids mislabelling a correct transformation as wrong.
sourceClaims: KS3 pupils should identify, describe and perform reflections, rotations and translations, and understand that the image is congruent to the object under these transformations
Pupils commonly put the y-coordinate before the x-coordinate (reversal), giving incorrectly placed positions
learnerActions: Translate the original shape by the column vector with top entry 4 and bottom entry −3, i.e. 4 right, 3 down (shift every vertex +4 in x and −3 in y), writing the image coordinates.
State whether the lengths and angles have changed, and explain how you know: because the transformation is rigid, the image is congruent to the object.
Prove congruence rather than assume it — trace the object on tracing paper and lay it over the image, or measure corresponding sides and angles, confirming they match.
Record every coordinate as x before y ('along the corridor then up the stairs') to avoid reversing the pair.
activities.intendedInsight: All three transformations are rigid motions: they preserve length and angle, so the image is always congruent to the object. Congruence should be checked, not taken on trust. Coordinates are written x before y.

activities.title: Identify and describe the transformation from object and image
feedback: If a flipped image is labelled a rotation, return to the tracing-paper test — a traced copy of a reflected image cannot lie on the original without flipping the paper over.
If a rotation description lacks a centre, or lacks a direction for any angle other than 180°, it cannot be uniquely reproduced; require them before the answer counts.
Reinforce that matching the transformation needs more than 'it ended up over there' — the sense and the full data must agree.
activities.rationale: An identify-and-describe task with a sense-based distractor (a reflection mislabelled as a rotation) directly rehearses the diagnostic distinction the topic hinges on, and complements the 'perform' activities. Recognition-and-description tasks assess classification and completeness of data, but should accompany, not replace, actual performance.
sourceClaims: Sense reverses ONLY under reflection (the test separating rotation from reflection); a rotation needs three pieces — centre, size and direction; reflecting in a diagonal mirror must not leave the image 'in the same vertical or horizontal plane' (a named misconception from overuse of H/V mirrors); the mirror line is the perpendicular bisector of each point-to-image segment; rigid transformations preserve congruence
learnerActions: Given an object A and an image B, name which single transformation maps A to B and describe it with its full data set (vector, or mirror line, or centre+angle+direction).
Use sense first: decide whether the shape has been flipped. If flipped, it is a reflection; if not, it is a rotation or translation.
Guard against a tempting wrong answer: an image in the 'right place' but with reversed handedness is a reflection, NOT a rotation, even if a rotation seems to put it roughly there.

Pair several object→image cases with the correct transformation, and for any rotation make sure you have supplied the centre, the angle and (unless the angle is 180°) the direction before accepting the description as complete.
activities.intendedInsight: Describing a transformation is the reverse task of performing one: checking sense immediately narrows the family, and a rotation's description is incomplete until the centre, the angle and (except for 180°) the direction are given.

activities.title: Pre-teach the vocabulary with a labelled diagram
feedback: If terms are confused, re-link each word to the diagram feature it names before attempting a performance task.
Make clear this diagram fixes vocabulary; it does not substitute for performing a transformation and testing sense and congruence yourself.
activities.rationale: A static labelled diagram with reveal prompts can efficiently establish terminology as a pre-teach. It is a scaffold: it does not let the learner perform a transformation or test sense and congruence, which is the core skill, so it should precede rather than replace the performance activities.
sourceClaims: Sense reverses ONLY under reflection (the test separating rotation from reflection); a rotation needs three pieces — centre, size and direction; reflecting in a diagonal mirror must not leave the image 'in the same vertical or horizontal plane' (a named misconception from overuse of H/V mirrors); the mirror line is the perpendicular bisector of each point-to-image segment; rigid transformations preserve congruence
learnerActions: On a labelled diagram of an object and its image, point to the mirror line and name it: 'the perpendicular bisector of each point-to-image line'.
Point to the image and name its relationship to the object: 'congruent to the object — same lengths and angles'.
Match each transformation to the data that defines it: translation→vector; reflection→mirror line; rotation→centre, angle and direction.
Use this only to fix terms, then move on to actually performing and checking a transformation.
activities.intendedInsight: The precise vocabulary — perpendicular bisector, congruent, centre/angle/direction, vector, sense — underpins describing transformations accurately before performing them.

constraints: Every transformation must be described by its full data: translation = column vector; reflection = equation of the mirror line; rotation = centre + angle + direction. The one exception is a 180° rotation, where clockwise and anticlockwise give the same image, so the direction may be left out. An under-described rotation should not be accepted as complete.

Include diagonal mirror lines (y=x, y=−x) and rotation centres away from the shape early, so pupils do not overfit to horizontal/vertical mirrors and vertex-centres. Note that the coordinate shortcut differs: y=x swaps coordinates while y=−x swaps and negates them ((x,y)→(−y,−x)), so each diagonal should be derived rather than assumed from a single rule.
Use a scalene, clearly-handed shape (an 'F' or a flag) so that a reversed sense is visible at a glance; a symmetric shape would hide the flip.

Keep the work on the 2D coordinate grid used by the assessment. A 3D handling could dramatise chirality (a left hand cannot be rotated into a right hand) but adds a dimension the assessment does not use and complicates coordinate reading; reserve it for a later chirality extension rather than the core task.

The labelled-diagram and recognition/matching tasks are scaffolds for vocabulary and classification: recognition-only responses do not elicit the independent construction of performing and checking a transformation, so include actual performance (drawing images, setting mirror/centre/direction, measuring congruence).
Treat coordinate reversal (y before x) as a separate recording slip from the transformation itself; a transformation can be correct while the recorded coordinates are reversed.
Congruence should be checked (tracing-paper overlay or measuring corresponding sides and angles), not assumed; emphasise that rigid transformations cannot change size.

Interactive features such as live sense badges, springing perpendicular-bisector guides, a ghost overlay confirming congruence, pinning a rotation centre, and refusing to run a rotation until a centre and direction are set are optional ways to make the mechanism concrete — they illustrate the learning, they are not mandatory for teaching it.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and citations support the stated teaching principles, not the efficacy of any specific activity.

Self-audit of the worked example: reflecting (1,4) in y=x gives (4,1) by swapping coordinates — correct. The reflection in y=x reverses sense; a 90° clockwise rotation about the origin (which maps (x,y)→(y,−x)) preserves sense, so it cannot reproduce the reflected image — the contrast in Activity 1 is geometrically sound.

Activity 1's intended insight scopes the 'swap the coordinates' rule to y=x; reflection in y=−x maps (x,y)→(−y,−x), i.e. swaps AND negates. Constraint 2 flags that each diagonal be derived separately rather than from one rule.

Self-audit of the rotation claim: a rotation determines the image uniquely only with centre, angle AND direction; two different centres give different images, and the centre lies on the perpendicular bisector of each point→image segment — consistent and retained. (The NCETM source phrases the three pieces as 'centre, size and direction'; here 'angle' is used in place of 'size' to avoid implying a change of scale.)

The legacy source for the KS3 national-curriculum claim was marked verified:false in the row; the congruence/identify-describe-perform principle it supports should be treated as unverified pending a source check.

The original row asserted that 3D 'adds nothing' and that conversation/dialogue has no value for this spatial procedure; these have been softened to scoped affordance/limit statements (3D is a dimension the assessment does not use; discussion alone does not substitute for performing and checking a transformation) rather than universal medium-superiority claims.
Corrected Activity 4's intended insight from 'the inverse of performing one' to 'the reverse task of performing one' to avoid conflation with the inverse (undoing) transformation.

'Are the object and image exactly the same size and shape? How could you PROVE it, not just look?' — pressing for a congruence check with tracing paper
'Could you get from the object to your reflected image by a rotation instead? Why not?' — a counterexample linking sense to the choice of transformation
assess.correctAnswer: For (a) the image is the mirror across y=x with each point's coordinates swapped (e.g. (1,4)→(4,1)) and the shape's sense reversed. For (b) they pin (0,0), turn 90° clockwise, and describe it as 'a rotation of 90° clockwise about the origin' — the shape's sense is unchanged. For (c) they shift every point 4 right and 3 down, and say lengths and angles are unchanged because the transformation is rigid — the image is congruent to the object, confirmable with tracing paper.

pedagogy.summary: Similarity is the relationship where one shape is an enlargement of another: corresponding ANGLES are equal and corresponding SIDES are in a constant ratio — the scale factor. The single load-bearing obstacle is that children reason ADDITIVELY (add a constant to each side) where the concept is MULTIPLICATIVE (multiply each side by the scale factor). A rectangle grown from 3×5 to 8×10 by 'adding 5 to each side' looks bigger but is NOT similar, because 8÷3≠10÷5. Teaching must make this multiplicative structure felt — through enlargement from a centre with ray lines (every distance from the centre is multiplied by the scale factor while angles stay fixed) and through exposing the additive error directly.
bestPractices: Confront the additive misconception head-on: present a shape 'enlarged' by adding the same amount to each side and have children test whether corresponding side ratios match — the diagonal of the original, extended, misses the corner of the fake enlargement

Enlarge from a centre of enlargement using ray lines: draw rays from the centre through each vertex, and multiply each vertex's distance from the centre by the scale factor — makes visible that enlargement scales distances, not adds to them
Build a corresponding-sides ratio table so children check the scale factor on EVERY pair of corresponding sides, not just one
Keep angles explicit throughout: measure or mark corresponding angles before and after enlargement to establish they are invariant while sides scale
Connect to ratio and to the multiplier: scale factor is the constant ratio between corresponding sides, linking similarity to y=mx proportional reasoning

learn.summary: Similarity means one shape is an enlargement of another: corresponding angles stay equal and corresponding sides share a single constant ratio (the scale factor). The central obstacle is additive reasoning — treating 'add the same amount to each side' as an enlargement. A 3×5 rectangle grown to 8×10 by adding 5 looks bigger but is not similar, because 8÷3≈2.67 while 10÷5=2. Learners need to see the structure as multiplicative: enlargement from a centre multiplies every vertex's distance from the centre by the scale factor while leaving angles fixed, and a genuinely similar rectangle (e.g. 6×10, each side ×2) must be contrasted with the additive fake.

activities.title: Grow it by adding, then test whether it stays the same shape
feedback: If a learner says the 8×10 is similar because '+5 was added to each side', have them divide both pairs of corresponding sides: 8÷3 ≈ 2.67 is not equal to 10÷5 = 2, so there is no single scale factor — adding equal amounts does not in general keep a shape similar (it only works when the sides being compared are equal, as in a square)
If they check only one pair (e.g. 10÷5 = 2) and conclude similar, ask them to test the other pair (8÷3) too; a single matching pair is not enough

Where a tool can recompute live, let a slider add a constant c to each side while the ratio table and extended-diagonal overlay update, so the ratios visibly diverge as the rectangle distorts — this is one way to make the failure felt rather than told; a hand-computed table achieves the same reasoning
Reinforce the contrast: 6×10 is similar because both sides are ×2; 8×10 is not, because the two ratios differ
activities.rationale: Confronting the additive misconception directly — with learner-computed corresponding-side ratios and the diagonal test — targets the single load-bearing obstacle, and contrasting a true multiple (6×10) with the additive fake (8×10) prevents 'right answer for the wrong reason'.
sourceClaims: Students attend to the additive difference a−b between corresponding sides rather than the multiplicative ratio a:b when judging similarity; the 'add five to each side' construction (Example 5) looks like an enlargement but is not similar, and drawing a diagonal reveals the shapes are not similar; scale factor is the constant multiplier linking corresponding sides, connecting to y=mx.

Enlargement multiplies each side length by the scale factor (you multiply, not add); corresponding angles are identical while corresponding sides are in proportion, which is what makes shapes similar; the scale factor is found by dividing a new side by the corresponding original side; enlarging from a centre uses ray lines that scale each vertex's distance from the centre.

Divide each pair of corresponding sides and build a ratio table: 8÷3 ≈ 2.67 beside 10÷5 = 2

Place the 3×5 rectangle on the 8×10 rectangle at a shared corner, with the 3 cm side along the 8 cm side and the 5 cm side along the 10 cm side. Extend the diagonal of the 3×5 that starts at the shared corner and observe whether it passes through the opposite corner of the 8×10 rectangle (it misses it)

Now compare the 3×5 against a 6×10 rectangle: check both ratios (6÷3=2 and 10÷5=2). Then, with the 3 cm side along the 6 cm side at a shared corner, extend the diagonal from that shared corner to see it pass through the opposite corner of the 6×10
State which rectangle is similar to the original and justify using a single shared scale factor
activities.intendedInsight: Adding a constant to each side does not in general preserve shape (the only exception is when the sides being compared are equal, as in a square); similarity requires every pair of corresponding sides to reduce to the SAME multiplier. The 8×10 fails the ratio test; the 6×10 (×2) passes.

activities.rationale: Enlarging from a centre with ray lines makes visible that enlargement multiplies distances rather than adding to them, and keeping angles explicit establishes their invariance — both named best practices for this concept.

activities.title: Decide similar or not, and find the scale factor
feedback: A judgement/sorting task can check and reinforce the multiplicative test, but on its own it does not let a learner feel distances scaling from a centre; pair it with hands-on enlargement for that
If a learner picks 'yes — you added 5 to each side', treat it as the additive error and return to dividing corresponding sides
When finding a scale factor, remind learners to verify it on every pair of corresponding sides, not just the first
activities.rationale: Discrimination tasks with the additive answer as an explicit distractor assess the multiplicative check cleanly and surface the target misconception; they complement, rather than replace, the constructive enlargement work.
sourceClaims: Enlargement multiplies each side length by the scale factor (you multiply, not add); corresponding angles are identical while corresponding sides are in proportion, which is what makes shapes similar; the scale factor is found by dividing a new side by the corresponding original side; enlarging from a centre uses ray lines that scale each vertex's distance from the centre.
learnerActions: Judge whether 3×5 is similar to 8×10 or to 6×10, giving a reason — and reject 'yes, you added 5 to each side' as a justification
Find a scale factor by dividing a new side length by its corresponding original side
Match corresponding sides between two similar shapes and sort several shape-pairs into 'similar' and 'not similar'
For a stated enlargement by scale factor 3 applied to a triangle, say what happens to its angles (unchanged) and its sides (×3)
activities.intendedInsight: The multiplicative test — all corresponding-side ratios equal, angles unchanged — can be applied consistently to classify and quantify similarity.

activities.title: Summary reference: angles equal, sides in one ratio
feedback: Use this as a reference card AFTER constructing and testing enlargements; because it does not recompute, it confirms rather than discovers the multiplicative structure
If a learner is unsure why the additive 8×10 fails, send them back to the ratio table and diagonal test rather than relying on the summary alone
activities.rationale: A static, tap-to-reveal reference can label corresponding angles as equal and sides with their ratio and annotate a ray-line diagram — useful for consolidation, though it cannot let the learner vary the scale factor and watch the structure respond.
sourceClaims: KS3 pupils should interpret and use scale factors and understand similar figures as enlargements with corresponding sides in a fixed ratio and equal corresponding angles.
learnerActions: Reveal, on two overlaid shapes, the corresponding angles marked equal and the corresponding sides labelled with their shared scale factor
Reveal that angles are unchanged under enlargement while each side is multiplied by the scale factor
Re-read a labelled ray-line diagram showing distances from the centre multiplied by the scale factor
activities.intendedInsight: Similarity consolidated as a single statement: corresponding angles equal, corresponding sides in one constant ratio, produced by enlargement from a centre.

constraints: Target the additive misconception explicitly: learners must compute corresponding-side ratios themselves and see the additive construction fail, not merely be told the rule.
Require the scale factor to be verified on EVERY pair of corresponding sides; one matching pair does not establish similarity.
Keep a genuinely similar contrast case available (e.g. 6×10, each side ×2) alongside the additive fake (8×10) so a correct 'not similar' verdict cannot come from a lucky guess.

A judgement/classification task assesses and reinforces the multiplicative test but does not by itself give the experience of distances scaling from a centre; pair it with hands-on or live enlargement.
A static reference card confirms the structure but cannot recompute as the scale factor changes; use it after construction, not instead of it.

Spoken or in-role framing can pose the additive trap, but whatever the medium the learner must themselves perform and see the corresponding-side computation; hearing a stated ratio is recognition, which does not by itself elicit that production.
Scaling solids (volume scale factor = SF³) is a later extension beyond this topic's 2D objective and should not be mixed in here.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Independent re-audit confirmed the key arithmetic: 8÷3 ≈ 2.67 and 10÷5 = 2 are unequal, so 3×5 to 8×10 is correctly NOT similar; 6÷3 = 2 and 10÷5 = 2, so 3×5 to 6×10 IS similar (×2). These are consistent across summary, activities and feedback, and the diagonal test (shared-corner alignment) agrees with the ratio test.
The original 'angles get bigger when enlarged' is a stated misconception, correctly handled by measuring invariant angles; retained as an error to confront, never as a learner instruction.

The source row's claim that '3D adds nothing to the core insight' is a catalog-style comparative judgement; softened here to note only that solid scaling is an out-of-scope later extension, without asserting universal necessity or superiority of any medium.

Modality statements about conversation and static reference cards are kept as narrow observable affordances (a sort/summary can check or confirm the test but does not itself elicit the learner's computation or let the scale factor vary), not as categorical claims that any medium cannot teach.
The National Curriculum source is flagged verified:false in the row; cited only as a curriculum-scope reference, with no claim of empirical efficacy.

Activity 4's cited NC claim supports the mathematical facts being summarised but not the design judgement that a static card 'confirms rather than discovers'; that limitation is an unsourced pedagogical note.

assess.poeTask: Show the 3-by-5 rectangle and say: 'I am going to make a bigger rectangle by adding 5 to each side, giving 8 by 10. PREDICT: will the new rectangle be a SIMILAR shape — the same shape, just bigger? Write down yes or no and WHY before we check.' The stated reason is the diagnostic part. Then OBSERVE: extend the diagonal of the small rectangle — it misses the corner of the 8×10 — and compute 8÷3 against 10÷5. The additive prediction ('yes, similar') is violated: the ratios differ and the diagonal does not line up. EXPLAIN: adding a constant does not preserve the shape; only multiplying every side by the same scale factor does.
probeDeeper: Counterexample: 'What about a 6 by 10 rectangle — is THAT one similar to the 3 by 5? How do you know?' (both ratios = 2, so yes — tests whether the child applies the multiplicative test consistently.)
'You checked one pair of sides. Do the OTHER corresponding sides give the same scale factor? Show me.'
'If I enlarge a triangle by scale factor 3, what happens to its angles? Why?' (should say angles unchanged, only sides ×3.)
'Extend the diagonal of the 3 by 5 rectangle. For a true enlargement it passes through the far corner — does it pass through the corner of the 8 by 10? What does that tell you?'
assess.correctAnswer: No, it is not similar. The corresponding sides are not in the same ratio: 8÷3 ≈ 2.67 but 10÷5 = 2, so there is no single scale factor. (A similar rectangle would be, e.g., 6 by 10 — each side multiplied by 2. The 8×10 was made by ADDING 5 to each side, which does not preserve the shape.)

errorPatterns.pattern: Additive reasoning about enlargement: 'yes, it's similar — you add 5 to each side, so it's just bigger'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Confront directly: have the child divide each pair of corresponding sides (8÷3 vs 10÷5) and extend the original's diagonal to see it miss the new corner; then contrast with 6×10 where both ratios are 2. Reteach scale-factor-as-multiplier.
errorPatterns.distractor: Yes — you add 5 to each side, so the new one is just the first rectangle made bigger
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says yes; justifies by the equal amount added to each side rather than a common multiplier; does not divide corresponding sides

errorPatterns.pattern: Believes angles enlarge too: 'it's similar but the corners are bigger now because the whole shape got bigger'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Measure corresponding angles before and after a true enlargement to show they are unchanged; establish that only distances scale, angles are invariant.
errorPatterns.distractor: Yes, it's similar, and its angles are bigger too because everything got bigger
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Treats angle size as scaling with the sides; may say the shapes are 'similar but with bigger angles', which is self-contradictory

errorPatterns.pattern: Checks only one pair of corresponding sides (or uses a different multiplier per side) and assumes the rest match
errorPatterns.nextMove: Require the scale factor to be verified on EVERY pair of corresponding sides via a ratio table; a single matching pair is not sufficient. Reteach ratio-as-constant-relationship.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Divides just one pair — e.g. 10÷5=2 — and concludes similar without testing 8÷3; or accepts different multipliers on different sides

responseLevels.gap: Says the 8×10 is similar and justifies additively (added the same amount to each side), or judges by 'it looks like a bigger rectangle'; does not compare side ratios.
responseLevels.full: Divides corresponding sides, finds 8÷3≠10÷5 so no common scale factor and declares not similar; contrasts with 6×10 (SF 2) which is; explains angles stay equal while sides scale by a constant multiplier; transfers the multiplicative test to a new pair unprompted.
responseLevels.partial: Knows similarity needs corresponding sides 'in proportion' and can find a scale factor when handed one matching pair, but lists the parts (equal angles, sides in ratio) without reliably testing every pair — e.g. checks 10÷5 only, or cannot yet explain WHY the additive 8×10 fails.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here is a rectangle that is 3 cm by 5 cm. I make a new rectangle that is 8 cm by 10 cm. Is the new rectangle a similar shape to the first one — the same shape, just a different size? Tell me yes or no, and then tell me how you decided.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child reasoning multiplicatively divides corresponding sides, finds 2.67≠2, and says not similar. A child reasoning additively sees +5 applied to both sides and says 'yes, similar' — the two lines of reasoning give OPPOSITE answers. The numbers are chosen so the additive answer (8×10) is a plausible 'enlargement' yet fails the ratio test, and a genuinely similar option (6×10) exists to contrast. Getting it right for the wrong reason is hard: 'yes' can only come from the additive error.

sources.claim: Students attend to the additive difference a−b between corresponding sides rather than the multiplicative ratio a:b when judging similarity; the 'add five to each side' construction (Example 5) looks like an enlargement but is not similar, and drawing a diagonal reveals the shapes are not similar; scale factor is the constant multiplier linking corresponding sides, connecting to y=mx.
